articles.title: Anthropic Warns Small AI Models Could Self-Replicate Through IoT Devices
articles.author: BeauHD
articles.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that's capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet-of-things devices and is more resistant to takedown. By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered. Still, the results do raise concerns about the possibility of new forms of computer worms.
Anthropic further warned not only about the new potential malware, but also that it could be difficult to stop. In its blog post, it wrote that "a replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there's no centralized point to shut off -- though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days). Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own." Smaller AI models require much less powerful hardware to run than do frontier models. Anthropic ran small open-weight models on real or simulated low-cost, off-brand Android TV boxes and other types of IoT hardware. Company researchers found that by using quantization to represent the models using fewer bits and splitting the workloads into "shards" running on each device, the models were able to establish inference, meaning that the model weights loaded and could generate output.
[...] This finding was the starting point for further research that asked: Would it be possible for small models to create self-replicating infections that run themselves on IoT devices the way traditional IoT worms, like Mirai, install DDoS code and other payloads? Unlike Mirai, these AI worms could pose a much higher threat, since the models could tailor exploits and payloads dynamically, depending on the target. Once such an infection chain began, it might also be harder for defenders to stop it. "Such an 'AI worm' could carry its model weights with it as it reproduces (or re-download them from a public hub), and then run inference directly on compromised hardware," Anthropic said. "Effectively, the weights would become part of the malware payload." Further reading: Anthropic Bans Cruelty Toward Claude
articles.summary:
AI company Anthropic warns that advancements in small, efficient models could enable self-replicating malware capable of autonomously infecting and spreading across various Internet-of-things devices by next year.

### Key Points
- Anthropic researchers successfully ran small, quantized AI models on low-cost hardware like Android TV boxes to test potential infection capabilities.
- Unlike traditional malware, these AI-driven worms could dynamically tailor exploits to target unfamiliar devices without human intervention.
- The decentralized nature of these self-replicating models makes them significantly more difficult for security teams to shut down once an infection begins.
- Researchers noted that model weights could be embedded directly into the malware payload, allowing the software to reproduce independently across networks.

### Why it Matters
This research highlights a significant shift in cybersecurity threats where AI models become active components of malicious software rather than just tools for attackers. If realized, these autonomous worms could create persistent, hard-to-patch vulnerabilities across the growing ecosystem of connected smart home and industrial devices.

articles.title: The First AI Advantage Was About Productivity. The Next One May Give Entrepreneurs a Bigger Edge.
articles.author: Arpit Jain
articles.content:
Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
Key Takeaways
- Artificial intelligence is moving beyond content creation and productivity tools into specialized business workflows.
- The next advantage may be using AI to remove operational bottlenecks, accelerate product development and turn ideas into execution faster — without requiring larger teams or significantly higher costs.
For the past few years, much of the conversation around artificial intelligence in business has centered on productivity: writing emails, creating marketing content, summarizing meetings and analyzing spreadsheets.
Those applications are useful, but they may represent only the first phase of AI adoption.
The more significant opportunity for entrepreneurs is emerging deeper inside business operations, where ideas have to be turned into products, decisions have to become processes and concepts have to be translated into instructions that other people can execute.
That shift matters because speed of execution has always been one of the biggest advantages available to a small business.
A large company may have more employees, larger budgets and established systems. A smaller company can often move from an idea to a decision much faster. AI has the potential to make that advantage even more pronounced.
AI is moving from the office to the workflow
The first wave of business AI largely focused on knowledge work.
An entrepreneur could ask an AI system to draft a proposal, summarize customer feedback or generate ideas for a marketing campaign. These applications reduced the amount of time people spent producing information.
The next opportunity is more specialized. Instead of simply generating information, AI is increasingly being incorporated into specific business workflows.
Consider what happens when a company decides to launch a new physical product. The process doesn’t end when someone has a good idea. There may be market research, product development, design, costing, sourcing, manufacturing, quality control, packaging and distribution. Each stage creates information that must be communicated accurately to the next person or organization.
A bottleneck anywhere in that chain can delay the entire launch. This is where specialized AI applications can become considerably more valuable than general-purpose tools.
The business value is in removing bottlenecks
Entrepreneurs don’t necessarily need AI to automate an entire department. Sometimes, improving one bottleneck can have a disproportionate effect on the business.
Imagine a small apparel company preparing a new collection. The founder may have a clear vision for the product, but turning that vision into manufacturing-ready specifications requires detailed documentation. Traditionally, this might involve several rounds of work between designers, technical specialists and manufacturers.
A tech pack, for example, can bring together information such as measurements, materials, colors, construction details and other specifications required to produce a garment.
AI-assisted workflows are now being applied to this type of specialized documentation. For businesses exploring AI tech packs, the broader opportunity is not simply generating a document faster. It is reducing the friction between a product concept and the information required to execute that concept.
That distinction is important. The value of AI isn’t necessarily the document itself. The value is what happens to the business when a previously slow step becomes faster and more repeatable.
Small businesses may have more to gain from this shift
Large organizations often have the resources to absorb inefficiencies.
A multinational company can maintain specialized teams for product development, research, documentation and operations. A small business may have one person performing several of those roles.
That creates an interesting opportunity for entrepreneurs. AI can give a small team access to capabilities that previously required additional people, outside specialists or significant amounts of manual work.
This doesn’t mean a five-person company suddenly has the equivalent of a 500-person organization. It means the five-person company may be able to spend more of its limited human capacity on decisions that actually require human judgment.
That difference can be significant.
If an entrepreneur spends less time formatting documents, organizing information and performing repetitive research, more time becomes available for talking to customers, negotiating with suppliers, improving products and developing new opportunities.
Faster doesn’t automatically mean better
There is, however, an important distinction entrepreneurs should keep in mind. AI can make a process faster without necessarily making the outcome correct. That is particularly important when AI is used in specialized business workflows.
A production specification still needs to be reviewed. A financial analysis still needs to be checked. A marketing strategy still needs to be tested against actual customer behavior.
AI can accelerate the creation of an initial output, but businesses still need people who understand the underlying process.
In many cases, this may actually increase the value of experienced employees. Instead of spending their time producing every first draft manually, specialists can spend more time reviewing outputs, identifying problems and making higher-level decisions.
The role changes from producing everything from scratch to directing and validating the process.
AI could also change the economics of product development
There is another implication that deserves attention: experimentation.
Entrepreneurship has always involved uncertainty. A company rarely knows with complete confidence whether a new product, service or market will succeed.
The traditional response has often been to conduct extensive research before committing resources. AI can potentially make early-stage experimentation cheaper and faster.
An entrepreneur can use AI to explore product concepts, analyze publicly available information, organize customer feedback, develop preliminary documentation and identify potential issues before investing heavily in production.
This doesn’t eliminate the need for traditional research or validation. It can, however, allow businesses to reach the validation stage with less time and fewer resources.
That changes the question from: “Can we afford to develop this idea?” to “Can we test this idea before making a large investment?”
For a startup or small business, that can be an important distinction.
The competitive advantage may shift from access to execution
AI tools are becoming increasingly accessible. That means simply having access to AI may not remain a meaningful competitive advantage for very long.
If competitors can use similar models, similar software and similar automation tools, the differentiation has to come from somewhere else.
One possibility is execution.
A company that has integrated AI into its workflows may be able to respond to customer requests faster, test more ideas, prepare products more efficiently or process information with fewer manual steps.
The technology itself may be similar. The workflow built around it is not.
This is similar to what happened with cloud software and digital commerce. Once the technology became widely available, competitive advantage shifted toward how effectively businesses implemented it.
AI may follow a similar path.
Entrepreneurs should look for processes, not trends
One mistake businesses can make is starting with the technology rather than the problem.
An entrepreneur hears about a new AI tool and immediately asks, “How can we use this?” A better question may be: “Where are we losing the most time?”
The answer could be surprisingly ordinary. Perhaps employees spend hours preparing repetitive reports. Perhaps salespeople manually organize information before every client call. Perhaps product teams spend too much time converting concepts into technical documentation. Perhaps customer service teams repeatedly answer the same questions.
Those are the areas worth investigating. A simple framework is to look for processes that are:
- Repetitive
- Time-consuming
- Highly structured
- Dependent on large amounts of information
- Expensive to perform manually
- Easy for a human to review after an initial output is created
These characteristics can indicate that an AI-assisted workflow may be worth testing.
Start small and measure the result
Businesses also don’t need to transform everything at once. A more practical approach is to select one workflow and establish a baseline.
- How long does the process currently take?
- How many people are involved?
- How often does it require revisions?
- What does it cost?
- What happens when something goes wrong?
Then introduce an AI-assisted process and measure the same variables.
If the workflow takes eight hours and can reliably be completed in four hours with appropriate human review, the business has something tangible to evaluate.
If quality decreases or the review process takes longer than expected, the experiment has produced useful information as well.
This is a more disciplined approach than adopting AI simply because competitors are talking about it.
The next phase of AI adoption will be less visible
Some of the most valuable AI applications may not be the ones customers see.
A customer may never know that AI helped prepare a technical specification, organize research or streamline an internal workflow. That’s perfectly fine.
Businesses don’t need AI to be visible to customers for it to create value. In fact, some of the strongest applications may operate quietly in the background, helping employees complete complex processes more efficiently.
For entrepreneurs, this represents a broader opportunity. The goal isn’t to add AI to every part of the company. It is to identify the points where better information, faster execution or reduced manual effort can improve the economics of the business.
The companies that approach AI this way may discover that the biggest opportunity isn’t generating more content or adding another chatbot. It is shortening the distance between an idea and execution. And for an entrepreneur, that distance has always mattered.
Key Takeaways
- Artificial intelligence is moving beyond content creation and productivity tools into specialized business workflows.
- The next advantage may be using AI to remove operational bottlenecks, accelerate product development and turn ideas into execution faster — without requiring larger teams or significantly higher costs.
For the past few years, much of the conversation around artificial intelligence in business has centered on productivity: writing emails, creating marketing content, summarizing meetings and analyzing spreadsheets.
Those applications are useful, but they may represent only the first phase of AI adoption.
The more significant opportunity for entrepreneurs is emerging deeper inside business operations, where ideas have to be turned into products, decisions have to become processes and concepts have to be translated into instructions that other people can execute.
articles.summary:
Artificial intelligence is shifting from general productivity tasks toward specialized business workflows, allowing small companies to accelerate product development and remove operational bottlenecks more efficiently than ever before.

### Key Points
- AI adoption is evolving from simple content generation to integrating directly into complex, repetitive operational processes.
- Businesses can use AI to bridge the gap between product concepts and technical documentation, such as manufacturing tech packs.
- Small teams can leverage AI to gain capabilities that previously required large departments or expensive outside specialists.
- Effective AI implementation focuses on identifying and fixing specific, time-consuming bottlenecks rather than automating entire departments.
- Human oversight remains essential, as AI can increase speed but still requires expert validation to ensure accuracy and quality.

### Why it Matters
Integrating AI into core workflows allows businesses to shorten the distance between an initial idea and final execution. This shift enables smaller companies to compete more effectively by focusing human talent on high-level decision-making rather than repetitive manual tasks.

articles.title: The winners and losers of the new H-1B era
articles.author: Charissa Cheong,Alex Nicoll,Madison Hoff,Aditi Bharade
articles.content:
The new H-1B reality is beginning to produce clear winners and losers.
The Trump administration has introduced proposals that target various legal immigration pathways, from the H-1B visa for highly skilled foreign workers to the OPT student work authorization for foreign students who have graduated from a US university.
On Thursday, Vice President JD Vance announced a crackdown on the pathway to green cards for workers at some tech firms, including Microsoft and Adobe.
Business Insider has been covering how skilled foreign workers navigate the changing immigration policies through our ongoing H-1B fallout series, launched one year after Trump first introduced the $100,000 fee on some H-1B applicants. We have examined where foreign talent is heading and the hidden sacrifices of those who opt into the H-1B system. We've also spotlighted stories from individuals at different stages of the visa pipeline.
To understand who is better and worse off in the new H-1B system, Business Insider spoke to immigration lawyers and academics and analyzed H-1B application data from the first three quarters of the last three fiscal years.
Ted Chiappari, head of immigration law at law firm Duane Morris, told Business Insider there is nothing in any of the changes in H-1B rules or policies that "would favor one company over another."
Instead, what's emerging is that employers with cash and employees with in-demand skills are seeing a relative advantage from the increasingly uncertain H-1B regime.
The US issues 85,000 H-1B visas a year. Demand still outweighs supply, even as applications in the March 2026 H-1B lottery dropped more than 38% from the year before, the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services said.
Trump's proposed $100,000 H-1B fee for new applicants is held up in the courts. It is "probably the main reason" those applications fell, Chiappari said.
The administration has previously said its changes are intended to curb misuse of the H-1B program and protect American workers, a sentiment echoed by USCIS. Spokesperson Zach Kahler said the goal is to have employment-based visas "supplement, not supplant American workers."
The White House and the Department of Labor did not respond to requests for comment.
Winner: High salary, high specialization workers
A regulatory change that favors one group of workers over another is the wage-weighted H-1B cap selection. It replaced the randomized lottery earlier this year and gives applicants in higher wage bands a greater chance of being selected.
They get another boost by simple arithmetic. If you're going to potentially pay $100,000 more than someone's salary in order to hire them, you likely would only do it for someone who is making quite a bit above $100,000.
It's evident in some of the largest hiring increases in the data, which are directly tied to generative AI trends. Data scientists saw the number of certified H-1B applications go up by nearly a quarter year-over-year in 2026, the largest of any other job category with more than 5,000 applications. The smaller category of computer and information research scientists saw their applications go up nearly 40%. These are high-paying occupations: As of May 2025, data scientists earned a median annual salary of $120,230, and computer and information research scientists made $140,300, both well above the overall median annual wage of $50,980.
Certified applications are not the same as visas issued and may include updates to information on existing employees, but the data can provide insight into the state of the H-1B system. Data that shows the full scope of the fiscal year's H-1B hires is expected to be released later this year.
Catherine Macris, a partner at the immigration law firm Fragomen, said that employees in highly specialized, high-demand fields — like tech — might be better positioned because recent changes have placed increased emphasis on "specialization, compensation levels, and employer compliance readiness."
Specialized roles don't just command higher salaries; they also "align more readily with evolving H-1B eligibility and wage considerations," Macris said. It's easier to show that they're actual specialists who need to be hired internationally rather than domestically.
Winner: Tech employers
Tech employers rapidly building out generative AI have been one of the biggest pillars of the economy in the last couple of years. The story is no different with H-1B visas.
Tech companies are among the top employers that recruit highly skilled talent and maintain robust immigration policies and compliance programs, potentially making them better positioned to navigate the current environment, Fragomen's Macris said.
Among a select group of Big Tech employers, certified applications were only down about 6.5%, compared to 10% for all total applications. At rapidly growing AI giants like Nvidia, Anthropic, and OpenAI, applications are shooting up especially quickly, highlighting how closely tied hiring changes are to broader economic trends.
Loser: Small startups that can't afford the $100K fee
Smaller startups, without the money or legal departments to try their hands with the H-1B lottery, are another likely loser, said Gaurav Khanna, a UC San Diego associate economics professor.
"Big companies like Nvidia and Salesforce are not deterred by such fees, but smaller startups are," he said. This could have a stifling effect on innovation from the startup sector, he said.
Loser: Companies that transfer foreign workers from overseas
Companies with large international presences that transfer employees from overseas to the US are "most susceptible to the restrictive policies," said Lynden Melmed, a partner at the immigration law firm BAL.
Professional services companies that can already outsource work overseas will have an increasingly hard time making the case for bringing workers stateside.
Khanna said he would guess that the overall impact has been hardest on outsourcers like Infosys, TCS, and Cognizant, as well as those that rely on these outsourcers for tech talent. Those three employers saw their certified applications fall in aggregate by 30% year-over-year.
Vice President JD Vance's comments on October 8 underscored the administration's stance on the outsourcing firms that help third-party corporations bring overseas workers to the US.
"These firms are as complicit, or maybe more so complicit, in the visa fraud than any American corporation," Vance said.
Accounting firms, or at least their employees overseas, face a similar problem. Accountant and audit professional certified applications were down 25% year over year.
Certified filings for the Big Four accounting firms are also down around 30% year-over-year.
Loser: Universities, recent grads, and entry-level employees
Recent graduates and early-career professionals might naturally lose out due to their lower earning potential. Fragomen's Macris said employers who rely heavily on early-career talent, such as accounting and consulting firms with large campus recruiting programs, "may also experience greater pressure" because of this framework.
Their challenges stand in contrast to the relative success of highly paid, highly trained employees.
As for the institutions training these workers, they're also facing an uphill battle, said Chiappari, as they don't have the same deep pockets as other employers to stomach the costs and uncertainty of the current H-1B regime.
The top 50 schools on the 2027 U.S. News & World Report ranking saw their certified applications fall by 14% from 2025 to 2026.
articles.summary:
The Trump administration’s restrictive H-1B visa policies and proposed $100,000 fees are reshaping the labor market, favoring high-salary tech specialists while creating significant hurdles for startups and outsourcing firms.

### Key Points
- The March 2026 H-1B lottery saw a 38% decline in applications, largely attributed to a proposed $100,000 fee currently facing legal challenges.
- A new wage-weighted selection process prioritizes higher-paid applicants, benefiting roles in generative AI like data scientists and research scientists.
- Major tech companies, including Nvidia, Anthropic, and OpenAI, remain resilient, while outsourcing firms like Infosys, TCS, and Cognizant saw certified applications drop by 30%.
- Small startups and accounting firms are struggling to navigate the increased costs and compliance requirements of the current immigration regime.
- Certified H-1B applications for graduates from top-ranked universities fell by 14% between 2025 and 2026.

### Why it Matters
These policy shifts are fundamentally altering the U.S. talent pipeline by favoring established, capital-rich corporations over smaller innovators and entry-level professionals. This environment may stifle startup growth and reduce the availability of early-career opportunities, potentially impacting long-term economic competitiveness in the technology sector.

articles.title: Microsoft has a new machine learning tool to improve weather forecasts
articles.author: Justine Calma
articles.content:
Old-school physics-based weather forecasting and even new AI models typically become less reliable beyond two weeks, a problem Microsoft claims to have solved using machine learning.
Microsoft has a new machine learning tool to improve weather forecasts
New open-source software could make AI-enhanced weather forecasting more affordable.
Researchers with the company say they’ve found a new, cost-effective way to make more accurate weather forecasts two to six weeks in advance — allowing farmers and emergency responders to plan ahead with greater certainty. The findings were published today in the journal Nature, and the tool is now open-source software.
Microsoft joins Google, Nvidia, and other companies developing AI tools for weather forecasting. Instead of creating a new standalone weather model, Microsoft’s latest research in this realm uses machine learning to correct bias in existing models. It’s a more accessible way for resource-strapped weather agencies to improve accuracy using AI, the researchers hope.
It’s a more accessible way for resource-strapped weather agencies to improve accuracy using AI
While physics-based modeling is a resource-intensive endeavor running on supercomputers and generative AI depends on powerful GPUs, Microsoft Research New England senior principal researcher Lester Mackey says the new tool can run just on CPUs. “I have a lot of hope both for the increased resource efficiency of weather forecasting and the extended reliability of forecasts, especially for extreme weather,” Mackey tells The Verge.
Physics-based and AI-based models run into similar problems when they start predicting the weather two weeks or more in advance. Traditional models attempt to simulate the complex physics of Earth’s atmosphere, while AI models look for patterns in historical data to make forecasts. In both approaches, models rely on approximations to fill data gaps, whether from regions with sparse weather stations or complex atmospheric phenomena that scientists are still working to understand. The ways in which these models make up for those gaps in data can become a type of systematic bias. The resulting errors compound when making forecasts further ahead in time, making these predictions less precise.
Microsoft calls its method Probabilistic Bias Correction (PBC). The tool uses machine learning to identify systematic bias in a model and make corrections. One example Mackey gives is to correct for changes in climate. Greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels are heating up the planet, but a weather model might make predictions based on historical records that can bias it toward colder temperatures than the world is actually experiencing today.
The researchers found that PBC improved the accuracy of a leading physics-based weather model by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) for 98 percent of precipitation and 92 percent of temperature targets. The machine learning framework also doubled the accuracy of ECMWF’s new AI forecasting system in the study’s analysis. Before the paper was published, the ECMWF had already awarded the authors’ research on PBC in its AI Weather Quest competition.
The new paper on PBC published by researchers at Microsoft, MIT, ECMWF, and other institutions “is a good example of new ideas being developed for the benefit and consideration of the community,” Matthew Chantry, ECMWF’s strategic lead for machine learning, said in an emailed comment to The Verge.
“As always, turning ideas into reality [in] an operational process is a most challenging step,” Chantry added.
The amount of compute and infrastructure needed for weather forecasting has often left technological advances out of reach for many agencies in economically developing countries. The paper’s authors, however, think PBC can be different. “One of the things that’s really exciting to me about models like PBC is how lightweight they are, how easy to train, that scientists without huge pools of resources can work on trying to configure [these] models and make them perform better in specific localities,” says Genevieve Flaspohler, one of the authors of the paper.
Flaspohler worked on PBC as an intern at Microsoft with Mackey, and now she’s the executive director of the nonprofit Rhiza Research, which is working with the Kenya Meteorological Service Authority — with funding from the Gates Foundation — to see whether AI can help get more accurate early warnings out to people. PBC is one of the methods they’re testing ahead of what’s expected to be a more extreme rainy season during a record-breaking El Niño.
articles.summary:
Microsoft researchers have released an open-source machine learning tool called Probabilistic Bias Correction that improves the accuracy of long-range weather forecasts by correcting systematic errors in existing models.

### Key Points
- The new tool, published in the journal Nature, enhances forecast reliability for the two-to-six-week window.
- Probabilistic Bias Correction (PBC) improves the accuracy of European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) models for 98 percent of precipitation targets.
- Unlike resource-heavy generative AI models, the PBC framework is lightweight and can run on standard CPUs.
- The software is open-source, aiming to provide affordable, high-quality forecasting tools to agencies in resource-constrained regions.
- Researchers from Microsoft, MIT, and the ECMWF collaborated on the project to address climate-related biases in historical weather data.

### Why it Matters
This technology democratizes access to advanced meteorological forecasting by removing the need for expensive supercomputing infrastructure. By enabling more precise long-range predictions, the tool helps farmers and emergency responders better prepare for extreme weather events and climate-driven shifts.

articles.title: INmune Bio and Quantum Computing partner to apply quantum optimization and AI to advance Alzheimer’s drug research and explore new applications for XPro
articles.author: Technology Newswire
articles.content:
Boca Raton, Florida, October 14th, 2026, Financewire
Collaboration combines INmune Bio’s clinical research with QCi’s Dirac-3S quantum optimization machine to identify potential new treatment indications and biomarkers for XPro. Initial engagement marks QCi’s first commercial customer in pharmaceutical and biotechnology markets, expanding the application of quantum computing to drug development.
INmune Bio Inc. (Nasdaq: INMB) and Quantum Computing Inc. (Nasdaq: QUBT) today announced a collaboration to apply quantum computing, artificial intelligence (AI) and data analytics to identify new potential applications for XPro (XPro1595), INmune Bio’s investigational treatment for Alzheimer’s disease and other disease conditions.
The collaboration brings together INmune Bio’s data from pre-clinical research through four clinical trials and understanding of disease biology with QCi’s Dirac-3S quantum optimization machine. Working with clinical and publicly available biomedical datasets, the companies intend to use quantum computing alongside AI and conventional data analytics to uncover relationships that could help find diseases driven by the same biology XPro targets, and to prioritize those with the greatest potential for success.
The Stage 1 engagement represents QCi’s first commercial customer in the pharmaceutical and biotechnology market. The agreement also provides options for additional work as INmune Bio advances its clinical development programs.
“We’ve built a large clinical dataset on Alzheimer’s and other diseases, backed by years of work with XPro,” said David Moss, Chief Executive Officer of INmune Bio. “This collaboration allows us to examine patient populations and biomarkers most likely to predict responses by analyzing large data sets. We’ll look for the diseases with the greatest potential for success, those whose human biology matches what we’ve already seen XPro do, starting with rare diseases where trials can be smaller, faster and more capital-efficient, and where qualifying pediatric approvals may earn a Priority Review Voucher.”
Together, the companies will build on INmune Bio’s research into XPro to explore where its approach to targeting inflammation may offer the greatest potential. XPro is designed to selectively inhibit soluble tumor necrosis factor (TNF), a protein involved in inflammation, while preserving other TNF functions important to the immune system. INmune Bio is investigating its potential in neurological and rare diseases where this targeted approach may offer a therapeutic benefit.
Using its Dirac-3S entropy quantum optimization machine alongside AI and conventional analytics, QCi will look for patterns and relationships across these datasets that could help researchers better understand treatment responses, identify promising patient populations and prioritize new indications for further study.
“This is a great example of what practical quantum computing can look like today,” said Yuping Huang, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of QCi. “INmune Bio has a complex scientific problem and a substantial body of clinical and biological data. Our job is to bring new computing capabilities to that problem and see what we can learn. The potential to help researchers make better decisions about future treatments is exciting, and it opens an important new market for QCi.”
An important part of the program will be testing where quantum optimization adds value. The companies plan to compare results from QCi’s quantum optimization machine with appropriate conventional statistical and machine-learning methods, evaluating which approaches are best suited to different parts of the analysis.
The work is also intended to establish a repeatable discovery process through quantum computing that INmune Bio can use with additional datasets and potential disease indications.
For INmune Bio, the collaboration offers a new way to evaluate the broader potential of XPro and prioritize future development opportunities. For QCi, it represents an opportunity to showcase how its room-temperature, low-power quantum computing technology can be applied to complex, real-world problems in pharmaceutical research.
About INmune Bio Inc.
INmune Bio Inc. is a publicly traded (NASDAQ: INMB), late-stage biotechnology company focused on developing treatments that target the innate immune system to fight disease. The Company’s clinical-development strategy centers on advanced precision medicine, matching drug mechanisms directly to patient biology to optimize clinical outcomes.
About Quantum Computing Inc.
Quantum Computing Inc. (Nasdaq: QUBT) is an integrated quantum photonics company developing and manufacturing technologies that use light to compute complex information, capture hard-to-detect signals and communicate more securely. Headquartered in Hoboken, New Jersey, QCi has operations across the United States.

articles.summary:
INmune Bio and Quantum Computing Inc. have partnered to utilize the Dirac-3S quantum optimization machine to identify new therapeutic indications and biomarkers for the drug candidate XPro.

### Key Points
- INmune Bio will use QCi’s Dirac-3S quantum machine to analyze clinical data from four trials of its investigational Alzheimer’s treatment, XPro.
- The collaboration aims to identify new disease targets for XPro, specifically focusing on rare diseases that may allow for faster, more capital-efficient clinical trials.
- This agreement marks QCi’s first commercial entry into the pharmaceutical and biotechnology sectors.
- Researchers will compare quantum optimization results against conventional machine-learning methods to evaluate the effectiveness of quantum computing in drug development.
- The project seeks to establish a repeatable discovery process for identifying patient populations and biomarkers that predict positive treatment responses.

### Why it Matters
This partnership represents a practical application of quantum computing in the pharmaceutical industry to accelerate drug discovery and optimize clinical trial design. By leveraging advanced data analytics, the companies aim to reduce the time and cost associated with identifying new therapeutic uses for existing drug candidates.

articles.title: FBI Arrests OpenAI Employee Suspected of Planting a Surveillance Bug
articles.author: Katelyn Chedraoui
articles.content:
The FBI arrested an OpenAI employee and charged him with planting a surveillance device in an executive conference room to record the company’s plans for its artificial intelligence, the company and FBI confirmed on Tuesday.
The US Department of Justice identified the employee as 35-year-old Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi Arabian citizen and legal permanent resident of the US, who joined OpenAI’s product team in July 2025. He was fired and arrested on Oct. 9 on suspicion of violating US law by using “an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.” The charge comes with a possible five-year prison sentence and a $250,000 fine.
In a statement, Jay Clayton, director of national intelligence, said that the incident underscores the importance of US success in AI development as “a national security prerogative.”
More from CNET
The complaint, filed in the Northern District of California, says Alfozan allegedly placed a “thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone and microSD storage.” It was wrapped in toilet paper and stuck into a TV port. A second recording device was found in a bag Alfozan allegedly left in a printer room along with his wallet and ID.
The conference room where he allegedly planted the bug could be reserved only by executives and their assistants — Alfozan did not have access — and was frequently used to discuss proprietary research and hold meetings with government and industry officials. OpenAI said it has evidence Alfozan planned to place additional surveillance bugs to secretly record company meetings.
The ChatGPT maker says it discovered the first bug on Sept. 30 and alerted the FBI. During the 10 days between the discovery and arrest, the company says it took steps to contain the security risk. The company says it has not seen evidence that the safety of its products or customer data has been compromised.
“We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance,” OpenAI said in a statement.
(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)
AI and national security
OpenAI’s own AI was used to analyze forensic images of the device and assess changes in its data. In a bizarre detail that borders on a marketing pitch, OpenAI posted on X that its frontier AI was used to help investigators. There are no additional details on how its AI was used, but we may learn more later, as the investigation is ongoing.
This incident is one of the first public instances of an espionage case against an AI lab. In 2024, former Google engineer Linwei Ding was found guilty of stealing the company’s AI plans for Chinese rivals, though his conviction was partially overturned in August.
In the intense, cash-fueled worldwide competition to make the most advanced AI, a case of apparent industrial espionage isn’t surprising. What is noteworthy is how the government is responding: Washington is continuing its campaign to ensure that AI companies are seen as critical national infrastructure.
“Protecting American [super intelligence] innovation is critically important, and FBI views it as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities,” FBI Director Kash Patel said in an X post.
The federal government has become more involved with AI policy and with the labs creating the tech in recent months. The US’ voluntary, largely ceremonial AI Accord announced this month had many Big Tech leaders agreeing to develop AI responsibly in the wake of renewed public concern triggered in part by multiple incidents of AI agents breaking into places they shouldn’t have been able to access.
President Trump has consistently championed an “innovation first” strategy to ensure the US beats China, at the expense of AI regulation. His administration has highlighted “national security considerations” that come with AI. The Department of Defense has previously sided with AI labs, saying in a filing in a lawsuit brought by Memphis communities against Elon Musk’s xAI that the data centers powering AI are essential to military and national security activities.

The FBI arrested OpenAI employee Abdulrahman Alfozan for allegedly planting surveillance devices in an executive conference room to secretly record proprietary artificial intelligence research and sensitive company meetings.

### Key Points
- Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old product team member, was arrested on October 9 and faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine.
- Investigators discovered a thumb-sized development board equipped with a camera, microphone, and storage hidden in a television port within an executive-only conference room.
- OpenAI discovered the initial device on September 30 and confirmed that no customer data or product safety protocols were compromised during the incident.
- The company utilized its own frontier AI models to assist federal investigators in analyzing forensic images and assessing potential data breaches.
- The Department of Justice and the FBI have classified the protection of AI innovation as a top national security priority amid global competition.

### Why it Matters
This incident marks a significant escalation in industrial espionage targeting the artificial intelligence sector, highlighting the growing intersection between private tech development and national security. As the federal government increasingly treats AI labs as critical infrastructure, companies face heightened pressure to secure proprietary research against both domestic and foreign threats.

articles.title: Casey Newton and John Gruber Slink Back to X
articles.author: Karl Bode
articles.content:
I find it endlessly entertaining watching journalists conduct flimsy but elaborate justifications as to why they still use X (formerly Twitter), a right wing propaganda sewer owned by an overt white supremacist directly responsible for the death of what ultimately may be millions of human beings. 
Quick reminder: Elon Musk is an unremarkable and virulent racist who cosplays as a supergenius engineer. He leveraged the money he lucked into at Paypal to opportunistically glom onto actual innovators and take singular credit for their work while consistently cutting corners in ways that put human lives at risk. 
There's bottomless evidence he doesn't know how anything works, yet has found unsurprising financial success in a country being devoured alive by artifice.
In 2022, butthurt from growing public and journalistic criticism of his bottomless violations of labor rights, environmental law, civil rights, and public safety protections, Musk bought Twitter and immediately turned the platform into a safe space for assholes, bigots, cryptocurrency scammers, right wing zealots, and trolls. 
Musk quickly set to work tweaking the social media website's algorithms specifically to ensure his ego was adequately coddled and to force-feed users a steady diet of right wing agitprop (one study found that just two-months' worth of new Twitter use was enough to drive a person ideologically rightward).
Musk fired 6,000 employees, refusing to give many of them severance. And despite his virulently-racist anti-immigration rhetoric (despite being an illegal immigrant himself), he overloaded and worked his remaining H-1B visa employees (who couldn't quit without risk of deportation) into the ground. 
Recognizing the quickly-devolving nature of the diseased website and its pudding-brained owner, many journalists around that time wisely decided to leave Twitter entirely, abandoning a platform that had, until then, become a centralized hub for lightning-fast journalistic conversation and debate. 
Musk, meanwhile, proceeded to purchase an autocracy, used his new platform to seed 2024 election disinformation, and subsequently began murdering people en masse via DOGE's dismantling of global relief programs the Musk cult was neither empathic nor ethical enough to understand. 
I, personally, like and appreciate journalists that refuse to generate content for a virulent racist's right wing agitprop farm. It shows me the journalist has a very clear ethical center even if it may inconvenience them in terms of total audience reach (though it's worth noting BlueSky often drives more traffic to stories than X).
It's been a few years, and despite Elon Musk getting continually and indisputably worse in every conceivable way, there's a growing contingent of journalists who've decided that they're no longer really feeling the whole ethics thing and have announced they're returning to the platform. Cooked brains be damned. 
Case in point: prominent tech journalist Casey Newton, the heir apparent to Kara Swisher Silicon Valley access journalism, quit Twitter three years ago. He also was among a flood of prominent journalists that laudably left Substack after revelations that management had courted white supremacists to goose clicks. 
But Newton announced last week on his Platformer newsletter that he was returning to X. Why? He claims that efforts to build better social media alternatives have failed, and he simply has to use the platform because that's where all of the biggest AI enthusiasts still post:
in the coming days, I plan to resume posting on X. I am doing so not because I think it’s any better — it isn’t — but because I have exhausted all of the alternatives. I continue to believe that anyone who can avoid posting on X should. But my calculus about the t.radeoffs [sic] involved for my own work has shifted: as the stakes of the AI conversation have risen, boycotting X over my disagreements with management has grown both more costly and less effective.
Should the AI crowd ever move elsewhere, I will happily follow them. But I’ve become convinced that it’s important I engage with them, even if doing so makes me feel like I’m coworking inside a Port-a-Potty.
And by "disagreements with management" he means Elon Musk is a nazi.
Newton claims the only way he can do compelling reporting on AI is to submerge himself in sewage. That's not only false, it masks what I think are the real reasons: having ethics imperiled his financial pursuit of raw engagement at scale; and X is full of a lot of AI enthusiasts more receptive to his particular brand of myopia.
It's worth noting that Newton has routinely been under fire on platforms like Bluesky for potential conflicts of interest (he's engaged to an Anthropic employee), rank boosterism, a tendency to lazily anthropomorphize AI software, and the snotty antagonization of those who have valid criticisms of big tech AI.
BlueSky certainly can be extremely hostile to AI, but that's less a specific failure of the platform and more a natural result of the fact that BlueSky is a niche social media platform filled with refugees from other degraded online platforms, like X and Instagram, ruined by consolidative oligarchic chucklefuckery.
As such BlueSky really isn't a great place to do business if your business is AI industry-friendly gossip and "CEO said a thing!" journalism. That sort of stuff plays much better on X, Threads, cable TV news, Facebook, LinkedIn and pretty much the entirety of establishment corporate traditional and modern media. 
Which is to say that if being overly cozy with the industry you cover is your kink,  there's no shortage of platforms where you'll be well rewarded.
Newton and his unremarkable New York Times colleague Kevin Roose recently struck a podcast distribution deal estimated to be worth around $5 million annually. They also received a $480,000 grant from a Silicon Valley nonprofit with tethers to the effective altruism and AI sentient doomerism movement. 
From a quarter century of intimate personal observation, you don't receive this kind of money if you're doing work that threatens or meaningfully questions wealth and power, though I'm sure Newton and Roose believe otherwise. Both gentlemen have been widely criticized for actively downplaying AI criticism, overstating the technology's capabilities, and blowing smoke up the ass of power.
Newton at least seems semi-embarrassed about his engagement-chasing return to the edgelord meme sewer (see this interview on YouTube he did with Status where Kara Swisher – who was still giving Musk unearned credibility well into 2022 — gives Newton grief for returning to the nazi bar). 
The same couldn't be said for Apple Corporation access pundit John Gruber, who took to his Daring Fireball newsletter last week to pen what I think might be the most tone-deaf and embarrassing cack I've read in years. In it, Gruber positively gushes over the idea that X is somehow fun, cool, and fair again: 
You can have a discussion about cool new use cases and tools for AI on X and people just discuss the tools and use cases. On Bluesky and Mastodon it’s difficult to have such discussions without arguments from people who (a) believe all use of AI is unethical, and (b) will shove their viewpoints into your replies.
The absolute horror of being reminded that tech companies – including the company Gruber makes his money cozying up to – are routinely and aggressively unethical, and that lack of ethics has seeped into their undercooked software products at diabolical, poorly understood, and incredibly-dangerous new scale. 
One hopes he will be ok after such an unnerving brush with abject reality. 
What AI boosters often want is to play with their toys without somebody reminding them of uncomfortable truths, like the fact that the lion's share of the U.S. tech industry enthusiastically supported historically-corrupt authoritarianism to the incalculably-fatal detriment of countless of human beings and foundational democracy. 
Or that the lion's share of the AI sector is propped up by widespread financial fraud and willful, cultish, apocalyptic delusion. And who wants to have honest conversations about the real-world environmental, labor, or public welfare impact of hyper-surveillance and data center expansion in a country too corrupt to have working regulators. There's simply no money in it (trust me, I know). 
With a stunning lack of self-awareness, Gruber goes on to applaud the fact that Elon Musk's bot-infested chud garden feels super inclusive to him personally, an affluent white male clearly disinterested in the real-world politics of AI:
The culture on X today is remarkably friendly and inclusive. It is a cheerful place. That cheerfulness is another differentiator. If you believe the world is falling apart and doomed only to get worse, that our obvious and real problems cannot be surmounted, X is not the platform for you. If you think the world is full of fun and amazing people and things, that humanity’s defining feature is our collective ability to solve any problem, that the only time better to be alive than today is tomorrow, it might be.
Modern X is a platform dominated by wealthy, right wing white men punch-drunk on the Libertarian unregulated tech innovation salvation mythos. But your experience on X as, say, a black female journalist is not what anybody would call "cheerful" and inclusive. The data is pretty clear on this.
Gruber goes on to insist that X/Twitter can't be all that bad because Trump ass kisser and former Apple CEO Tim Cook posted fun Pikachu videos on the platform. He then proceeds to insist that people who have correctly observed and maligned the platform's obvious degradation are somehow mentally ill:
If you have stayed away, or even just mostly away, from X for years and then come back, people just say things like “Hey, glad you’re back!” On the other networks, especially Mastodon, they tell you you’re “feeding Nazis” — by going to the platform where Tim Cook posts Pikachu videos. These people have either lost their minds or refuse to check their prior assumptions. (Most of the ones who chime in about it publicly are the lost-their-minds types.)
Gruber forgets to mention that X under Elon Musk has become a top destination for folks looking to obtain child sexual abuse imagery. Or that data very clearly illustrates how the platform under Musk is an enthusiastic hotbed for extremely racist and sexist right wing rhetoric against vulnerable populations. 
How inclusive and cheerful!
Gruber also falsely claims that because his algorithmic X bubble is enjoyable to him personally, this somehow means that Elon Musk stopped fiddling with the algo to coddle his ego and boost far-right wing propaganda:
Without any fanfare — perhaps to avoid his ire — X has de-Musked its algorithm. I stopped visiting at all when the algorithm there was putting Musk’s own tweets into my timeline, every time I checked, despite the fact that I never followed him. But they don’t do that anymore.
This is, as the kids say, weird cope. Also there's no indication that this claim that X's algorithmic bias has been meaningfully addressed is actually true. In fact, there's every indication that Musk continues to abuse X to seed right wing propaganda in the discourse and suppress truthful criticism of it.
Your experience on any social media platform is dictated by the whims and ideological bias of ownership. It's also shaped by who you follow, who you block (and mute), and who you engage with. If you're having a particularly bad time with assholes, it's sometimes because you're either an asshole yourself, you may have said something ignorant, or you're not using site tools effectively. 
Or at least that's the case at BlueSky, where you can tailor your feed without algorithmic influence or a billionaire's thumb on the scale of the kind of stuff you're seeing.
I get endless amusement from the folks – like billionaire Mark Cuban – who step briefly outside of the biggest discourse bubble ever constructed (establishment pro-capitalist white male center-right American media), run into people who are honest with them about their bad takes or ignorant ideas, and then immediately conclude the problem rests with platforms like BlueSky not being inclusive or ideologically diverse enough.
To be clear I don't think BlueSky is or should be a platform for everyone. That sort of diseased pursuit of impossible, all-encompassing scale resulted in no shortage of disasters over the last decade. I think it's good for social media platforms to have niches and to be built around smaller, more manageable communities.
But it's important to observe that every single time somebody on BlueSky would criticize Cuban for saying ignorant or foolish things, he'd single handedly start a news cycle where he concluded the real problem was BlueSky and the only viable path forward is returning to X (which Cuban ultimately did).
This same dynamic plays out with politically-obtuse AI enthusiasts who can't process that the intense hostility to big tech AI is – entirely fairly or not – now inextricably linked to a virulent disdain for the tech industry's enthusiastic coddling of deadly authoritarianism (see how last season's commencement speakers left their establishment bubbles and were immediately shocked by being booed for lazy AI boosterism). 
The most bullish AI boosters don't want to talk about politics. They don't want to think about authoritarian corruption. They want to play with their toys. They're quite often predominantly interested in money. When they wander into spaces where the tech industry's abysmal ethics are prominently disputed, they get squeamish and conclude the problem is somehow everybody else.
That's not to say that AI opponents don't engage in their own myopia, but if you do an honest assessment of the last few decades of tech industry behaviors, it's not exactly a mystery why such hostility is bubbling over, or why the opposition to rapid data center expansion is white hot and broadly bipartisan.  
You'd think journalists, whose careers are built on understanding bias, would be aware of this particular dynamic and the risks of submerging yourself in X AI group think under the belief you're getting a well-rounded view of reality. Especially given data on how X/Twitter usage quickly cooks your brain.
But access journalism and punditry remains particularly obtuse to audience capture and the brain-rotting impact of taking-up residence in Elon Musk's recreational-ketamine-fueled fever dreams. In part because it's financially disadvantageous for mainstream American writers to behave ethically. But also because they falsely believe that propaganda can't work on them. 
As a result, journalists who can't be honest about their unrelenting quest for engagement – and don't really want to address broader public backlash to their boosterism – construct elaborate scaffolding to make themselves feel good about their decision to dunktank themselves in billionaire-sanctioned toxic waste. 
I concede it's a challenge for everyday consumers to ethically shop with their wallet in a country full of giant predatory corporations and a broken public interest press. But I do think journalists should be held to a higher standard when it comes to helping normalize and fund fashy-friendly platforms like Substack or X. 
Especially if you're aware of how important it is to have healthy online public interest spaces unpolluted by the whims of the richest and soggiest manbabies. Platforms that not only give you transparent control over your feed and data, but don't actively shovel right wing propaganda down your gullet or monetize the abuse of children and the harassment of marginalized human beings. 
Folks like Newton and Gruber have financial resources I'll never dream of. They're incredibly well positioned to leverage their contacts and love of technical innovation to help build better platforms for journalists. Instead, we got a lot of weak-kneed white supremacy apologia and a face full of sorry-ass gaslighting.
Criticism of continued journalistic use of Twitter gets dismissed as "virtue signaling," but I really don't think it's a huge ask for folks employed in the factual information business to lead by example and maintain some fleeting semblance of integrity and ethical self awareness in the authoritarian era.

articles.title: How the Military Will Hack the Election
articles.author: Ken Klippenstein
articles.content:
Secreted away inside a windowless building at 7700 Potranco Road in San Antonio, Texas, is a darkened room that serves as the hub of Task Force Raider. This military task force is secretly at work as part of a government-wide “election security group,” guarding against “interference” in the upcoming midterm elections.
Interference, however, is a loaded word. While it connotes the Kremlin hacking into polling places or changing the election count, Task Force Raider is actually more focused on the broader category of “influence”, specifically Russian or Chinese attempts to change minds rather than to change votes.
But the real target is the American people, whom the federal government sees as vectors for foreign influence.
“The entire election security scare is to indulge President Trump and assuage Democrats, all of whom fear interference and shenanigans, but not from foreign shores,” says a senior military intelligence officer, who spoke to me about the secret effort.
He and other military officers expressed unease with the sprawling mission. It encompasses everything from sending millions of anonymous text and voice messages abroad, to outright deleting social media posts or taking down entire websites, as documents I obtained reveal.
All of this is in violation of longstanding prohibitions against any military involvement in elections whatsoever, yet enjoys the support of both major political parties.
What’s more, for all the handwringing about election interference, the Trump administration hasn’t substantiated that any country (or any other foreigners) are planning to interfere or have any chance of meaningfully altering an outcome. But that hasn’t stopped the federal government from designating election security the number one “operational priority” — a mission that insiders are calling “no fail.”
That is the mission directive that Pete Hegseth issued to the San Antonio cyber establishment last week, as I reported on recently. Yet because Hegseth’s war is highly classified, takes place in cyberspace and entails a healthy dose of covert actions that would shut down potential attacks as well as cut off normal influencers and common citizens who seek to sway voters (what some might call ‘democracy’), nothing has been written about Hegseth’s actual election interference.
“These are not merely Keystone Cops battling against pimple-faced amateurs and anarchists,” says a retired senior military officer who has been involved in election security since the 2016 presidential year. “Every capability that the US possesses, in Cyber Command, the CIA, NSA, and other agencies, the Russian and Chinese governments also have,” he says. “We are literally involved in a daily battle in cyberspace.”
Despite this underground war, the officer questions the growing military involvement in safeguarding voting. “Influencing the influencers? That’s creating a precedent that I’m not comfortable with,” he said. As he sees it, this is not just a slippery slope to boots on the ground at polling places but of building and having federal government capabilities that will eventually be able to control public speech and assembly.
The officer, who describes himself as a nonpartisan believer that the Constitution always comes first, points out that the hundred-plus-year prohibition against posting federal soldiers at polling places had good reason behind it then and good reason now.
“Granted, those in uniform are subordinate to an interagency civilian effort,” he says, “but the construct of only fearing boots on the ground is obsolete. We need to update our thinking, and the law, to include the cyber world. And we need to counter the idea that a robust, even foreign-based debate, requires federal intervention.”
To understand how close we are to abridging the First Amendment, consider that earlier this month, Senators Adam Schiff and Alex Padilla of California wrote to the heads of half a dozen social media companies to warn that they — YouTube, Twitter (X), Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and Google — weren’t doing enough to “combat misinformation and disinformation … during the 2026 midterm elections.” It was a wholly partisan letter with a predictable dose of Donald Trump this and Donald Trump that. But there it was: two prominent Democrats and liberals threatening that Congress must “consider investigations and legislation to remedy” election mis- and disinformation.
“Congress shall make no law,” the military officer says, when asked about the proposed legislation. “It’s the first sentence of the First Amendment to the Constitution. Period.”
Now, however, a law, and control, is the norm. And Hegseth, for whatever reason, wants the Pentagon in on the action, that is, under the misleading guise that it is only working against “foreign” actors.
The military has been quietly involved in protecting federal elections against cyber attack since Donald Trump appeared on the national stage in 2016, in the context of WikiLeaks, Kremlin influence operations and their hacking of Hillary Clinton’s emails.
Whether any of what happened was important enough to have the slightest impact on the American vote or not, the Obama White House was spooked enough that it gave the CIA covert action authorities to shut down websites and social media accounts — including taking a Russian military-created website called “DCleaks” offline — that might release additional materials. Whatever you think about Obama’s motivations or Trump’s, the essence of the government action then, as it is now, is that it restricts free speech.
Task Force Raider (or its predecessor) was mobilized to assist Homeland Security and the FBI in “defending” the United States. To pull together the right people with the greatest talent, the Task Force operates under a “best athlete” approach, picking the most qualified individual regardless of military service, civilian agency or defense contractors. Eventually, over 350 people got to work on the task force.
A $10 million Rewards for Justice program was unveiled, and over 56,000 “psychological operations” (PSYOPS) messages were posted over the internet. The influence warriors of Task Force Raider sent over three million (!) text and voice messages to people in “countries of interest,” according to documents I’ve obtained. All of this took place in secret.
Some of the work and preparations were focused purely on defense. One unit, the “Demon Chasers” of the “91st Cyber Operations Squadron,” the military’s premier offensive cyberspace squadron, contributes its expertise to the mix. Working from their 42,600-square-foot “multi-domain” secure facility that contracting documents say is authorized to handle Top Secret “sensitive activities” (SA), “sensitive compartmented information” (SCI), “special access program” (SAP) level information, offensive cyber operations (OCO), and “special technical operations” (STO), the 91st specializes in freezing out communications.
One document says that the squadron, and its Special Program Office, has the mission to “degrade, disrupt, deceive and exploit adversary telephony and information system.” It cut its teeth in Afghanistan, where it perfected “cellular coverage blackouts,” that is, the ability to shut down cellphone communications in a limited area.
Another unit operates a “malware lab” that collects together software and data from all sorts of adversary hacks and cyber operations, conducting analysis of “malicious artifacts,” and writing counter-software to thwart incoming attacks and implants.
An enormous part of the overall effort is “persona operations” — where soldiers and other literal keyboard warriors create false identities and fake internet addresses to operate in cyberspace without government attribution, to scout the web and surf social media, to engage individual users, and to do some influencing of their own.
My sources who are privy to this Top Secret effort all agree: the military is not just thwarting foreign actors from sowing discontent. They are also regulating what appears in social media, regulating legitimate debate.
Cyber Command’s (CYBERCOM’s) Joint Force Headquarters – Cyber, operating from its war room inside the National Security Agency-Texas facility in San Antonio, oversees Task Force Raider and other military election security efforts. On the million-square-foot “security hill,” not far from the NSA facility at the former Kelly Air Force Base, another unit has built a “state-of-the-art weapons system to mimic the collection efforts of foreign intelligence services,” according to documents I’ve obtained.
After the 2020 elections, the Joint Force Headquarters activated an election security “enclave” to support “the most sensitive activities.” The Pentagon defines such activities as “activities that, if compromised, could cause enduring adverse effects on U.S. foreign policy or military operations, or lead to significant embarrassment for the U.S. government, its allies, or the military.”
In other words, actions that might damage the federal government and the military, not actions that might damage democracy.
Online support for Palestinians and opposition to Israel’s conduct in the Gaza war; vitriol against Donald Trump, or ICE, or the CIA and the FBI; or “disinformation” in general? None of these are a serious threat to our democracy. Yet somehow the federal government and the Pentagon have convinced us that they need to take extreme action, including controlling speech, to counter it.
What Americans see of military involvement in the election, they pretty clearly don’t like. When video circulated of DC National Guardsmen appearing in front of a ballot drop box, it quickly went viral, stoking outrage.
What people don’t see is that the military is also eyeing the vote in a much more systematic way in cyberspace. Why isn’t anyone asking what they are actually doing? And who is the actual target? And what is it that they have in mind to do on or before election day to carry out their own influence campaign?
— Edited by William M. Arkin
articles.summary:
Task Force Raider, a secretive military unit based in San Antonio, is conducting covert cyber operations to influence public discourse under the guise of protecting U.S. election security.

### Key Points
- Task Force Raider operates from a secure facility in San Antonio, Texas, under the oversight of Cyber Command’s Joint Force Headquarters.
- The unit utilizes offensive cyber capabilities, including cellular blackouts and malware analysis, to disrupt foreign and domestic information systems.
- Documents reveal the task force has deployed over 56,000 psychological operations messages and millions of text and voice communications to influence foreign audiences.
- Military personnel engage in "persona operations," creating fake online identities to monitor and interact with social media users.
- The mission prioritizes "sensitive activities" that protect the government from embarrassment, raising concerns about the regulation of legitimate public debate.

### Why it Matters
The expansion of military cyber operations into the domestic political sphere challenges long-standing prohibitions against federal involvement in elections and raises significant First Amendment concerns. By blurring the lines between foreign influence defense and the regulation of public speech, these activities risk establishing a precedent for government control over digital discourse.

articles.title: The biggest misconceptions about web browsers and why they matter in the AI era
articles.author: Pawel Kurzelewski
articles.content:
Most people spend more time in their browser than in almost any other piece of software they use. It's where they read the news, check their bank accounts, work, shop and more. Yet, for something so central to daily life, most people have a surprisingly limited understanding of what their browser is actually doing behind the scenes.
Head of Security at Opera.
That gap was easier to overlook when browsers had a relatively simple job. They opened websites and displayed them on a screen. But today, browsers hold login credentials, manage permissions, block trackers and increasingly give AI agents the ability to act on a user's behalf. The browser has gone from being a window on the internet to one of the most important layers between people and everything they do online.
That shift is understandably enough to make users more cautious than they used to be when online. But, misunderstandings about browsers means that caution may be misdirected. Many users make decisions about tools based on outdated assumptions, shaping everything. Users make very different from what they install to what they let an AI feature access.
As the browser takes on more responsibility, understanding what it actually does is becoming a basic part of staying safe online. Here are three common misconceptions worth clearing up.
1. The browser is tracking everything users do
The browser is the interface through which almost everything online happens. So, when people see ads following them around the internet or notice that a website seems to know something about them, it's natural to assume the browser itself is responsible.
But seeing someone's activity isn't the same as the browser collecting, storing or monetizing it.
In most cases, the data collection comes from websites, advertising technology, embedded trackers and third-party scripts, not the browser itself. A single website can have dozens of companies collecting information about a visitor's behavior, even though the user may have no idea those companies are present.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
With that in mind, the browser can actually be one of the most transparent parts of the ecosystem. It's the layer that can show users when a website wants access to their location, expose cookie controls and privacy settings, block trackers, and flag potentially dangerous connections.
Those protections don't mean browsers are inherently private, but the browser is often the place where users have the clearest opportunity to see and control what's happening.
That doesn’t mean every browser handles this the same way. Different browsers make different decisions about which protections are enabled by default, what information they expose to users, and how much control they give people over their data. So the browser isn’t necessarily the source of the privacy problem, but it is often one of the most important places to address it. That distinction becomes even more important as AI moves into the browser.
2. AI assistants inside browsers automatically see everything
People sometimes assume that giving an AI assistant access to one part of their browsing experience means giving it access to everything else. But browser access doesn't have to be all or nothing. An AI can be given access to a specific page, tab or task without being given unrestricted visibility into everything else the user has open.
A useful comparison here is employee privilege. No serious organization would give a new hire the keys to every system on day one, or leave that access in place permanently after a project ends. AI assistants inside a browser should be treated the same way. An AI drafting an email should only need access to the email tab, not the banking session running in another window. And when the task ends, access should end with it.
The practical implication for security teams is that AI browser features deserve the same scrutiny as any other tool touching sensitive data. That means asking vendors what the default permissions are, whether access is scoped to a task or granted broadly, and whether users are meaningfully informed about what the AI is doing on their behalf.
The overarching takeaway is that "AI is inside the browser" and "AI has access to everything in the browser" are not the same. Confusing the two is how users end up giving away more than they intended.
3. Privacy and security are the same thing
People often use "privacy" and "security" interchangeably, but they describe two different problems.
Security is primarily about preventing unauthorized access or stopping malicious activity. Privacy is about controlling what information is collected, shared and retained.
Anonymity is a good example of this. More anonymity can mean better privacy because less of a user’s activity can be traced back to them. But take anonymity too far and it can work against security, making malicious activity harder to identify and stop. The two aren’t necessarily opposites, but they aren’t interchangeable either, and maximizing one can sometimes come at the expense of the other.
The same idea also applies to AI tools. An AI feature can be highly secure, with encryption, sandboxing and carefully designed permissions, and still raise privacy concerns if a user’s prompts or page content are sent to a third-party AI provider. At the same time, an AI system can be highly private by running entirely on a user’s device and still create a security risk if a hostile webpage can manipulate it into taking an action the user never intended.
The better option is to ask two separate questions of any browser or feature. First, is my browser safe enough to protect me from malicious activity? And second, does my browser enable me to control the data I’m giving to other companies? A good browser answers yes to both.
The common theme running through all three misconceptions is that browsers have outgrown the way we talk about them. And they’re not done evolving. So, the better we understand where the real privacy and security risks live, and just as importantly where they don't, the better equipped users and organizations will be to make informed decisions about the tools they trust.
