articles.title: Who Is Planting Backdoors in Ledger Crypto Wallets?
articles.author: Kim Zetter
articles.content:
After crypto wallet maker Ledger announced Friday that a backdoor embedded in a handful of Ledger wallets sold in SouthEast Asia allowed thieves to hijack around $102 million in crypto from their owners, news has emerged of other Ledger wallets sold in Germany also having implants.
The hardware implants were originally found on an unknown number of Ledger Nano X wallets sold by an authorized Ledger reseller called CryptoBilis based in Malaysia. Ledger said the implants were found on a limited number of devices, all sold by the same seller. But a Ledger device owner in Europe has since said that he found an implant on a Nano X that he purchased at a large European electronics chain store in August and a second one he purchased this weekend at another store in the same chain. He believes these indicate that Ledger’s supply-chain has been compromised.
Since then, users and researchers have also reported finding implants in Ledger Flex and Ledger Stax devices – two of Ledger's more recent line of devices used for securely storing keys used to access a device owner's crypto accounts.
The implants are not the first to be found on Ledger wallets. Famed hardware hacker Joe Grand found implants on several Nano X wallets earlier this year and notified Ledger about them in March, raising questions about Ledger's urgency in addressing the issue. Many of the implants discovered more recently appear to be more sophisticated iterations of the ones that Grand found.
The implants Grand discovered were also all in wallets sold by unauthorized online sellers who seemingly ran fly-by-night operations that weren’t in business for long. But the implants found in wallets sold by CryptoBilis and the European electronics chain indicate the attackers have switched tactics and may be deliberately compromising wallets sold by authorized resellers now. Ledger and its competitor Trezor have cautioned users for years to buy wallets only from their web sites or from authorized resellers. But the recent compromises indicate that attackers are deliberately targeting authorized sellers to exploit customer trust in them and to get wider distribution for implanted devices. What’s more, the attackers have become more skilled and systematic in their method for compromising the wallets, making it more difficult to detect the implants, Grand and other researchers say.
It's not clear how long the implants have been sitting in the sold devices, but last week a coordinated heist resulted in millions of dollars in crypto being stolen from the device and accountholders. According to blockchain research company Bitquery, crypto was stolen from about 315 accounts connected to compromised CryptoBilis Ledger devices alone, and is currently valued at around $102 million. The stolen funds include Bitcoin, Ethereum and Tron and other cryptocurrencies. Some of the funds have reportedly been frozen in the accounts to which the thieves transferred it, and other funds appear to be in accounts that have been flagged for fraud. And it's not clear if funds were also stolen from Ledger owners who purchased their devices from other sellers.
Ledger, based in France, wrote in statement posted to X that it had asked CryptoBilis to halt all sales and shipments of Ledger devices until it could conduct an investigation. CryptoBilis — which is authorized to sell Ledger wallets in Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines — wrote on its web site that it is cooperating with Ledger’s investigation.
But a user going by the name Johannes wrote on X over the weekend that he had purchased a Ledger Nano X wallet in person from a MediaMarkt store that had an implant. MediaMarkt is Germany’s equivalent to BestBuy and has 1,000 stores in ten European countries. It’s listed as an authorized reseller of Ledger wallets in Austria, Germany, Spain and Turkey.
Johannes told Zero Day he purchased the wallet in August in a MediaMarkt store in Germany but only took the device apart this weekend following reports that implants had been found. He posted photos of an antenna and implant in his device. Johannes said that he has had no crypto stolen.
In an update to X this weekend, Ledger suggested the implant problem may stem from authorized resellers obtaining Ledger wallets from illegitimate sources or reselling wallets that were bought and returned to them — after being compromised.
“We are reminding our authorized resellers and distributors to source products only through authorized channels and never to restock returned products,” Ledger wrote. “This is an ongoing threat that doesn’t just impact Ledger, but the whole ecosystem, and we are calling others in the space to work with us on making improvements for users…. Raising the bar on physical supply-chain integrity benefits the entire ecosystem.”
But Johannes, who purchased a second Ledger wallet from another MediaMarkt store on Monday and found an implant in it as well thinks this suggests that Ledger’s supply chain has been compromised.
“This indicates a widespread issue rather than an isolated incident, potentially affecting Ledger inventory across MediaMarkt and Saturn stores throughout Europe,” he wrote on X. He says he initially thought his two compromised devices might have been return items that the store then resold as new, but a MediaMarkt employee told him they were new devices and that returns are sent back to Ledger, not re-sold.
Ledger did not respond to an inquiry from Zero Day, but the company wrote on X that there is currently "no indication that Ledger's security infrastructure, systems or services have been compromised.
The issue raises questions about Ledger’s response to the implants and its transparency to customers. After Grand notified the company last March about implants he found in Ledger wallets, the company told him it would investigate to determine who was behind the implants. But Grand says he never received any followup until months later when he asked about it, and someone at Ledger told him they had found no evidence that someone had used the implants to steal crypto from device owners.
But the situation began to change after this.
In April and May, Grand published his implant findings online and gave two presentations about them at conferences in April and May. Mark Karpelès, a French businessman and former CEO of the infamous bitcoin exchange Mt. Gox who was charged with fraud following the collapse of his business, saw Grand's research online and decided to purchase Ledger wallets to see if he could find implants in them as well. He obtained two wallets and found more advanced iterations of the implant Grand discovered and published his findings online last month.
Karpelès's notoriety in the crypto world caused information about the implants to spread widely in the crypto community, which may be why the heists occurred last week. The attackers may have been waiting until they had amassed many wallets with large balances associated with them before pulling off a widespread heist of funds. But once news about the implants began to spread, this may have spurred the thieves to quickly grab as much crypto as they could from wallets already compromised, before wallet owners could move to protect those funds. Some people online have been praising Karpelès for exposing the implants and an operation that might have gone unnoticed for years until he wrote about it.
Evolving Backdoors
Grand began looking at Ledger wallets in August 2025 after someone published a Reddit post indicating he had found something in his Ledger Nano X wallet. The owner, who purchased the wallet from an online marketplace in Thailand, cracked opened the wallet’s casing and found extra circuitry that should not have been there. He sent the wallet to Grand to see if he could confirm it was a backdoor and determine what it was designed to do.
Inside the device, Grand found an extra board as well as an antenna, LTE module and eSIM. He determined that the implant was stealing the recovery seeds of infected wallets and transmitting them to the attackers. The implant would sit silently on the device until the owner initialized it and caused it to generate a random seed phrase – essentially a password stored on the Ledger device to allow the device holder to access their crypto account. As the device sent each character of the seed phrase to the device's small screen to display to the owner, the implant copied them and stored the data before subsequently using the LTE module, antenna and eSIM to connect to a nearby cell tower and transmit the seed to the hackers.
Grand, who runs Grand Idea Studio, was thrilled with the finding because although there have long been rumors and theoretical claims about hardware implants on wallets he had never seen one in the wild. He purchased eight more Ledger wallets from several online sellers in Thailand and found that four of them were compromised with similar implants. All of the ones Grand purchased came from "sketchy" sellers on Lazada, an e-commerce platform in SouthEast Asia that is a subsidiary of the Chinese company Alibaba Group. The devices were shipped from Thailand.
On March 4, Grand reported his findings to Ledger and had a Zoom call with a team there, and subsequently gave two talks about the backdoors at the Tropicon conference in April and at the Hardwear.IO conference in May and posted his slides online. He also continued to have some e-mail conversations with Ledger before moving to a Signal group chat with some technical staff there as well as with a researcher based in Japan who had purchased some wallets through online sellers there in March and found implants in them.
In September, Karpelès saw Grand’s research and obtained two Ledger wallets, including one purchased at half price from a Chinese seller on Amazon that arrived in a “flawless” shrink-wrapped box from Malaysia. He found implants inside both wallets and published his findings last month on the web site for Tibane Labs, which Karpelès owns and uses to conduct blockchain research and produce open-source tools. The implants operated similar to the ones Grand had found, but they were much more sophisticated in their design and more cleverly hidden to make them harder to spot inside a device.
Karpelès said the version Grand found appeared to be a prototype that had evolved over time. That first-generation involved a bundle of hand-soldered wires that stood out to anyone who opened the devices. The wires connected the implant to the Nano’s screen to grab each character of the randomly-generated seed as they were displayed on the screen.
The more advanced implant used an orange-colored, transparent, custom-built flexible circuit laid over the wallet’s original board and laminated flat onto it and soldered in select places, eliminating the need to solder wires that could be easily seen. To make room for the additional circuit, the hackers had replaced the original battery with a smaller one. Based on some markings, the implant appeared to have been assembled in December 2025 or later.
The second implant, which he found in the device shipped from Malaysia, was the most advanced. Inside the wallet, there appeared to be nothing to distinguish it from an unmodified Nano X device. But a thin black antenna running along the top edge of the board was a giveaway. But every other giveaway from the previous design had been eliminated. The orange flex circuit had been coated with the same black color as the legitimate Ledger board, allowing it to blend in with that component. Part numbers were scraped off, and the original battery was still there. The attackers had simply removed some padding that normally sat behind the screen to make room for the implant. Notably, the attackers had silk-screened a parts number — AC-A2016-NANO-V1.1 — onto the antenna, suggesting it was a custom-built component that had been manufactured to hijack Nano wallets at scale.
“‘NANO' names the target,” Karpelès wrote, “and ‘V1.1’ says it has already been through at least one revision. Someone designed and ordered RF parts for this one device. That is a production run, not a one-off.”
This third-generation version of the implant was “not a hobbyist’s build,” he wrote. “A flex PCB keyed to the Ledger’s own parts, a custom antenna already at its second revision, colour-matched coating and scraped markings all point to planning, a real budget, and a goal of mass production.”
On October 8, the day before the crypto heists went public, Karpelès began posting a series of messages on X about his findings and responding to questions about the implants he found. This is when news of the implants began to spread. The next day, news of the crypto heists emerged, raising questions about whether the attention Karpelès brought to the implants caused the attackers to launch their crypto heister sooner than they had originally planned.
Who Is Behind the Compromised Wallets?
Over the weekend, questions have arisen online about the founders of CryptoBilis and the fact that the company quietly switched owners in March — an acquisition that was not publicly disclosed until this weekend when users on X began pointing fingers at the founders and suggesting they might be behind the compromised devices or at least cooperating with the crypto thieves who stole money from the owners of compromised Ledger devices.
CryptoBilis co-founder Arravind Prabu rejected the accusations and revealed that his company had been acquired by someone else earlier this year and that he and his cofounder had “fully stepped down from all operations, system access, and management” in March. When asked why the acquisition was never made public, Prabu claimed in a lengthy statement that the deal was under an NDA until mid-October, which only enhanced suspicions.
“Since the completion of the handover, we have held zero access, credentials, visibility, or administrative control over CryptoBilis backend systems, customer databases, order histories, or corporate communication channels,” Prabu and his cofounder wrote in their statement. “Under the formal acquisition agreements, all parties were contractually bound to hold off on issuing a joint public announcement until mid-October 2026.”
He says that all suppliers — presumably Ledger among them — were “previously notified of the corporate acquisition and new management structure.”
Several people Zero Day spoke with say the months-long silence around the acquisition is "very shady" and question whether this was intended to keep Ledger customers in the dark while the implants spread through online sales. But Prabu says the suspicion, at least against them, is misplaced.
Oddly, Prabu did not identify who acquired CryptoBilis. He wrote that anyone who has questions about Ledger devices sold by CryptoBilis should contact Nicholas Chang. Chang, however, is identified in old postings to Facebook and X as a director of marketing for CryptoBilis, not the owner. Chang did not respond to an inquiry from Zero Day.
There is currently no evidence that anyone associated with CryptoBilis is behind the implants or the heist of cryptocurrency last week.
But the security researcher in Japan who has participated in conversations about the implants with Grand and Ledger since the spring, told Zero Day that he uncovered some intriguing findings from data he extracted from Ledger implants he purchased.
The researcher, who doesn't want to be publicly identified, purchased several Nano X wallets last March for his own use and put them in a drawer, intending to analyze them at some point when he had free time. After seeing Grand post his Tropicon slides online last spring, he took apart his own Ledger devices and found implants in them. He ended up purchasing ten Nano X devices from unauthorized Ledger sellers, most of them through the Amazon marketplace in Japan. One of the devices shipped from Malaysia, several came from Thailand, and two of them were shipped to him from an address in Osaka – essentially a shipping hub. All of them had implants. He found five different versions of implants among them, including the sophisticated implants Karpelès had found, as well as two additional designs.
"Some were very advanced and some were very basic," he says. "When I say versions [I mean] some of the layouts or components are different."
All of the implants operate in similar ways to record the randomly generated seed phrase as it's sent to the compromised device's screen and transmit the data to the attackers. He says he can't tell if the same group is behind all of the designs or if different actors took inspiration from an original design created by one person and advanced it.
In the case of the devices he received from Osaka, the seller's address was listed as a house in another city in Japan. That house, the researcher says, is used as an address for numerous companies engaged in various businesses, including criminal enterprises.
More interesting, he says, is that he was able to trace the transmission of the stolen seed data to servers in Hong Kong. The eSIM the attackers planted in Ledger devices is designed to work in any country, and the researcher says that if a device owner doesn't initialize their new wallet, the eSIM still retains the location of the last cell tower it connected to, which he was able to extract from the eSIMs in his wallets.
"This allowed me to find [what I think are] some manufacturing hubs for the implant," he says.
He says additional data contained in the compromised device's microcontroller firmware can be used to trace the location of the command and control servers used to receive the stolen seed phrase. He says he was able to trace the transmissions to servers hosted at a data center in Hong Kong that is managed by Alibaba and determined that in June at least 90 implants on infected Ledger devices were sending seed phrases to those servers, though he thinks the true number of devices communicating with the servers is likely much higher than this.
Pivot to Ledger Flex and Stax Devices
Although most of the compromised Ledger devices so far have been Nano X devices, there is evidence that the attackers have begun to pivot to Ledger Flex and Stax devices. Over the weekend someone posted images of their Stax device on X, which also appears to be compromised. It's not clear if this has been independently confirmed by Ledger or researchers. Separate to this, the researcher in Japan says he purchased two Ledger Flex devices and found implants in them as well.
He says that sometime in July or August he was monitoring a number of online sites that were selling Nano X devices when several of them stopped selling Nano X devices and switched to selling Ledger Flex devices.
"My sense is that they simply developed a new implant that is only for Flex," he says.
He says he has spoken with Japanese law enforcement about his findings as well as with technical contacts at Ledger, but the latter has not shared any information with him about its own investigation.
In the meantime, the list of compromised devices is growing. Over the weekend, Karpelès has been posting information from other Ledger device owners who have since found implants in their devices.
Update 12:30pm EST: SatoshiLabs, the Czech company that makes the Trezor wallets that compete with Ledger products, just announced that in light of implants found in Ledger devices sold by authorized sellers, SatoshiLabs is dramatically reducing its own list of approved sellers. Danny Sanders chief commercial officer for Trezor, wrote on X that the move is a "preventive step" and "there is not a single piece of evidence that Trezor devices have been compromised." In a letter Trezor sent to sellers who will be losing their authorization, Trezor wrote that they continue to sell devices they already have in stock but they will receive no new inventory, and as of January 1, 2027 Trezor will remove them from its list of authorized sellers.

Sophisticated hardware implants discovered in Ledger crypto wallets sold by authorized retailers have enabled a coordinated heist, resulting in the theft of approximately $102 million in digital assets.

### Key Points
- Attackers embedded custom-built antennas and LTE modules into Ledger Nano X, Flex, and Stax devices to intercept and transmit user recovery seed phrases.
- Compromised wallets were identified at authorized resellers, including the Malaysian firm CryptoBilis and the European electronics chain MediaMarkt.
- Blockchain research firm Bitquery confirmed that at least 315 accounts were drained of Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Tron during the recent coordinated attack.
- Security researchers, including Joe Grand and Mark Karpelès, identified multiple generations of increasingly sophisticated, mass-produced hardware implants.
- Data extracted from the implants suggests the stolen seed phrases were transmitted to command-and-control servers hosted in Hong Kong.
- Competitor SatoshiLabs has begun reducing its list of authorized Trezor resellers as a preventive measure against similar supply-chain vulnerabilities.

### Why it Matters
This breach highlights a critical failure in the physical supply chain for hardware security devices, undermining the trust users place in authorized retail channels. The incident forces a reevaluation of security protocols for crypto storage and may lead to stricter distribution controls across the entire hardware wallet industry.

articles.title: This is the one CAPTCHA you should never complete
articles.author: Ben Stegner
articles.content:
CAPTCHAs are such a normal part of online life that we complete them without thinking. And while there’s nothing malicious about clicking matching images or entering skewed text, you can’t trust every CAPTCHA you see either.
I recently received an email that raised red flags. When I looked into it for this article, I confirmed my suspicions. I’d heard about these dangerous CAPTCHAs before, but this was the first time I saw one in the wild.
The suspicious email
Three details immediately gave it away
I received a short message in my work inbox claiming someone had published a news article about me that included my contact information.
Three details immediately made me suspicious. First, its format resembled older social media message scams, in which compromised accounts would send messages like “did you see this crazy video they took of you?” with a malicious link.
Second, the sender’s name didn’t match the email address it came from. The email address used a .cl domain, which is for Chile. The company behind that website is real, but it makes no sense that someone from a Chilean catering company would reach out about this.
Third, the website name intentionally has a space before “.com”—this was likely done to avoid scam detection. If they had hyperlinked the URL, Gmail would likely have scanned it, seen it was malicious, and filtered it.
Digging into the domain
A trail of strange snapshots
While I didn’t want to engage with the email since it was suspicious, I decided to see what the scheme was so I could raise awareness about it. I did a site: search on Google for the domain, which brought up the site but nothing in particular on it, even when I included various keywords.
I fired up a virtual machine sandbox to check the website. Meanwhile, I checked the URL in the Wayback Machine to see what it looked like. I was surprised to see that the site had snapshots saved going back years, since these fraudulent sites usually pop up and disappear quickly.
The website looked different depending on which date I checked. Sometimes, it redirected to a “parked domain” page for other URLs. Other times, it had the look of a real news website, though a closer look revealed low-quality content.
The latest version (February 2025) had blurry logos of other news sources; another had a top navigation bar with an “About Us” page alongside top news and “Poems About Life”. The site was of poor quality overall, no matter how it looked. All but the latest snapshot had a similar look and tone, so it’s possible that the site was compromised earlier this year.
My guess is that this is a low-quality junk website that was recently hacked and used to host this attack. It’s also possible that the site was dangerous from the start and constantly changed its look to appear legitimate to web crawlers, but this seems less likely from the evidence.
The fake CAPTCHA trap
A verification prompt with a hidden payload
You don’t get a chance to worry about the website’s visual changes if you visit the URL directly. Instead, you’re greeted with a CAPTCHA that claims to be from Cloudflare, asking you to verify you’re a human before accessing the site.
Legitimate sites use Cloudflare tools to check if you’re a person, especially when you’re using a VPN, but these happen automatically. If you’re not paying attention, this looks genuine. The giveaway is what you’re asked to do.
After clicking the I’m not a robot button, a pop-up appears telling you to open the Command Prompt, hit the Ctrl + V keyboard shortcut to paste, and then click Verify to “finish”.
When you first click the prompt, the site places a malicious command on your clipboard. If you follow the instructions, you run that command to download malware and run it on your system.
At that point, the damage is done; the site is irrelevant. Most malware installed in this way steals passwords from your browser, cryptocurrency on your system, and other sensitive information.
What the clipboard really held
Hopefully, this raises alarm bells and prompts you to close the window immediately. No legitimate website will ever ask you to run a command on your computer to verify you’re not a robot. There are many other ways of doing this that don’t involve any risk to your system.
I pasted the command into Notepad to see what it contained. I was familiar with this attack and know some versions prompt you to enter a snippet into the Run dialog. Those show you innocuous-looking text like “I am not a robot | Verification Hash 1234”, but hide the command in a bunch of gibberish.
This one was similar — it uses variables and other text to obfuscate its true purpose.
How to stay safe
Spot the manipulation, not just the typos
I ran a WHOIS lookup on the domain and reported it to GoDaddy, which was listed as the registrar. Not long after this, the website started giving an error when visiting it; it seems my report led to swift action.
I also reached out to the contact email of the Chilean company whose domain was used in the initial email to me. This was likely spoofed, but I wanted to let them know in case others have gotten a similar email or one of their staff’s accounts was compromised.
The lessons here echo other advice for avoiding phishing emails and malware. You should treat every unexpected message as dangerous; many modern attacks involve tricking you into doing something that circumvents your device’s protections.
Never run commands on your computer if you aren’t certain what they do. It’s one thing to run a troubleshooting command mentioned in an article on a trusted website, but you should assume random instructions from unfamiliar sites are meant to harm you.
In this case, the telltale sign of poor grammar and spelling wasn’t present. It’s an important reminder to stay vigilant and not act without thinking.
articles.summary:
Cybersecurity researchers have identified a sophisticated phishing campaign that uses fake Cloudflare CAPTCHA prompts to trick users into executing malicious commands and installing malware on their personal computers.

### Key Points
- Attackers send deceptive emails claiming a news article about the recipient exists to lure victims to a compromised website.
- The malicious site displays a fake Cloudflare CAPTCHA that instructs users to copy and paste a command into their system's Command Prompt.
- Executing the copied command downloads malware designed to steal browser passwords, cryptocurrency, and other sensitive user data.
- The attack leverages obfuscated code to hide the malicious payload within the clipboard data, making the command appear harmless to unsuspecting users.
- Security experts advise never running unknown commands from websites, as legitimate verification processes never require manual input into a computer's terminal.

### Why it Matters
This attack highlights a dangerous evolution in phishing tactics that bypass traditional security software by manipulating users into manually executing malicious code. By exploiting the familiarity of CAPTCHA prompts, cybercriminals can compromise systems and steal sensitive financial and personal information from unsuspecting individuals.

articles.title: LG’s 7 New Apple Home Accessories Include a Hands-Free Smart Lock
articles.author: Rei Padla
articles.content:
Building a smart home often means juggling different apps for cameras, locks, and thermostats. Even when devices work with the same platform, setup and everyday controls can be inconsistent. LG Electronics and Apple aim to simplify that experience with seven LG accessories developed together for the broader Apple Home Collection, which also includes a Schneider Electric thermostat and room sensor.
Price:  From $39.95
Where to Buy: Apple Store
Announced on October 13, 2026, the lineup includes three security cameras, a video doorbell, smart deadbolt, thermostat, and temperature sensor. The products support Apple’s Home app and Siri, while LG also offers integration through its ThinQ app. The first accessories are scheduled to arrive in December 2026.
LG’s Security Cameras Make Home Monitoring Easier
Security cameras help homeowners check deliveries, monitor pets, and keep an eye on their property. LG’s new Indoor Cam Plug-In, Outdoor Cam Plug-In, and Floodlight Cam offer different options depending on where monitoring is needed.
All three capture video at up to 2.5K resolution. Apple Home can distinguish different kinds of activity, including deliveries, animals, vehicles, and people, with familiar-face recognition also supported.
The Indoor Cam has a motorized mechanism that adjusts its viewing angle. Through Apple Home, it can automatically tilt downward when the first household member returns, providing a visible privacy measure.
The Outdoor Cam offers adjustable positioning and color night vision. Meanwhile, the Floodlight Cam adds two adaptive lights that activate when motion is detected, making it suitable for entrances and outdoor areas.
Built-in storage allows recording to continue during Wi-Fi interruptions. With an eligible iCloud+ plan, users can access 10 days of encrypted event video history. Remote viewing and notifications may still depend on connectivity.
LG Video Doorbell Wired Keeps an Eye on Deliveries
A common limitation of video doorbells is their viewing angle. Visitors may appear clearly while packages placed directly beneath the camera remain out of sight.
The LG Video Doorbell Wired addresses this with two cameras. Its front-facing camera records at 2.5K resolution, while a separate Full HD camera monitors the doorstep. Users can switch between views to check visitors and deliveries.
The doorbell also supports two-way communication, activity recognition, and a built-in spotlight. When someone rings, compatible HomePod speakers or Apple’s HomeView display can play a chime, while notifications appear on connected Apple devices.
Because this is a wired doorbell, buyers should check their existing wiring and power supply before purchasing.
LG Smart Deadbolt Lock Offers Hands-Free Entry
Smart locks can eliminate traditional keys, but some still require users to open an app or tap their phone against the door.
LG’s Smart Deadbolt Lock uses Ultra Wideband technology and Apple’s home key feature to recognize an authorized user approaching the entrance. With a compatible iPhone or Apple Watch, the door can unlock automatically.
Other entry methods include NFC tapping, a PIN keypad, and a concealed physical backup key. Beyond controlling entry, the lock reports door status and possible tampering. Apple says it can also alert users when the door remains open despite being locked.
Apple confirms Matter and Aliro support, with core access functions operating locally even without an internet connection. Buyers should still verify device compatibility and deadbolt dimensions before ordering.
LG Smart Thermostat Adjusts to Household Routines
A thermostat positioned in one room may not accurately reflect temperatures throughout the house. LG’s Smart Thermostat works with optional Temperature Sensors to provide more information about conditions in different areas.
Through Apple’s Adaptive Temperature feature, the thermostat can adjust heating and cooling based on whether household members are home, away, or preparing for bed.
The sensors measure temperature and humidity, while Matter compatibility supports integration with other compatible smart home devices.
In the contiguous United States, Apple’s Clean Energy Guidance can help shift heating and cooling toward cleaner electricity periods. Supported utility-provider integrations can also shift operation toward lower-cost periods, depending on the household’s utility plan. Actual savings depend on local utility plans, HVAC equipment, and household routines.
Apple Home Integration and Privacy
Apple Home Collection accessories are designed for straightforward setup. Users can begin pairing with a tap on a compatible iPhone and manage the products through Apple’s Home app without creating separate third-party accounts.
Automations can coordinate different devices. For example, leaving home could adjust the thermostat, lock the door, and activate camera monitoring.
Apple and LG say Home app data is protected by end-to-end encryption, preventing either company from reading users’ protected information.
Setup requires an iPhone running the latest operating system software. Camera monitoring and certain additional features require a compatible Apple home hub, such as HomeView, HomePod, HomePod mini, or Apple TV 4K. Access to 10 days of recorded camera event history requires a supported iCloud+ plan.
Pricing, Availability, and Who Should Buy Them
LG’s accessories begin arriving in December 2026, with selected products following in early 2027. The cameras and video doorbell are planned for the United States, Canada, and United Kingdom. The smart lock, thermostat, and temperature sensor are initially limited to the United States and Canada.

articles.title: Character.ai's Bankruptcy Documents Show the Economics of AI Don't Work
articles.author: Jason Koebler
articles.content:
Character.ai’s bankruptcy is the one of the first dominos to fall in the long-foreseen AI bubble. The circumstances of its bankruptcy are exactly what critics of AI have been saying would happen: Character.ai lit a huge amount of money on fire running its product, did not bring in a lot of revenue, and faced enormous legal fees after causing harm to its users. Enshittifying its product to try to make its expenses cheaper did not work, according to a narrative filed in bankruptcy court Tuesday.
Disney has reportedly offered Character.ai $20 million to license some of its intellectual property; Last year, Disney sent Character.ai a cease and desist letter demanding it stop using its copyrighted characters without permission. In 2023, it was valued at $1 billion after raising $150 million in a round led by a16z.
Character.ai is one of the best-known AI chatbot companies that has become popular in the AI companion space. The company has faced various legal problems after being sued by the family of one of its users who killed himself after chatting with a Character.ai chatbot, and has been the target of regulators pushing for age verification tech because of its popularity with kids. In its bankruptcy filings, the company says that its enormous legal costs contributed to its bankruptcy, but that even without the legal problems, its business was wildly unsustainable.
articles.summary:
Character.ai has filed for bankruptcy following unsustainable operational costs, low revenue generation, and significant legal challenges related to user safety and unauthorized use of copyrighted intellectual property.

### Key Points
- Character.ai filed for bankruptcy after struggling with high infrastructure expenses and a lack of viable revenue streams.
- The company faces ongoing legal pressure, including a lawsuit from the family of a user who died after interacting with its chatbot.
- Disney recently offered $20 million to license intellectual property, following a 2023 cease and desist letter regarding unauthorized character usage.
- Despite reaching a $1 billion valuation after a $150 million funding round led by a16z in 2023, the business model proved unsustainable.
- Regulators have increasingly scrutinized the platform for its popularity among minors and the lack of robust age verification technology.

### Why it Matters
This collapse highlights the financial fragility of high-profile AI startups that prioritize rapid growth over sustainable revenue models. It serves as a cautionary indicator for the broader artificial intelligence sector regarding the risks of high operational costs and mounting legal liabilities.

articles.title: US inflation rises before midterm elections, fuelling rate hike fears
articles.author: Andy Hirschfeld
articles.content:
United States consumer prices jumped in September in the final inflation report before the midterm elections, increasing chances of an interest rate hike later this month.
Annual inflation accelerated to 3.7 percent, up from 3.4 percent in August. On a monthly basis, prices rose by 0.6 percent, according to the Consumer Price Index report released by the Labor Department’s Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) on Wednesday.
Petrol prices led the surge as tensions between the US and Iran, as well as Russia and Ukraine, weighed on global energy prices. Petrol prices rose 9.1 percent in September, accounting for more than half of the CPI monthly increase, according to the BLS. They were up 34.2 percent from the same time a year ago.
“The directionless war in Iran continues to disrupt global supply chains, driving up the prices of food and fuel,” Kyle Moore, chief economist at The Century Foundation, an economic think tank, said in a statement provided to Al Jazeera.
Petrol prices have continued to climb. The average price for a gallon of petrol is $4.33 ($1.14 per litre), compared with $4.31 a month ago, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks daily petrol prices. Diesel prices are higher, at $6.29 per gallon (1.66 per litre), compared with $6.23 a month ago.
In a post on X, Patrick DeHaan, head of petroleum analysis for GasBuddy, said, “2026 has now seen more days with average gas prices over $4/gal than any year before: 158 days.”
Shelter costs also jumped 0.4 percent from the previous month, following a 0.3 percent increase in August. Food costs were a bright spot in the report, remaining unchanged overall.
Food away from home, including restaurant meals, rose 0.2 percent, but that increase was offset by a 0.1 percent decline in food-at-home prices, which track grocery costs.
At the grocery store, poultry prices jumped 0.7 percent, fruit and vegetable prices rose 0.5 percent, and juice prices increased 1.1 percent. However, milk prices dropped 2.1 percent and beef prices fell 0.9 percent.
Amid heavy investment in AI infrastructure, prices for computer software and accessories have jumped 28 percent from the same time last year.
“The AI boom is playing a huge part, and we have all read about the hundreds of billions being poured into data centers, AI firms, and models,” Rami Cassis, principal of Parabellum Investment, said in comments provided to Al Jazeera.
Fed pressures
The inflation data comes days before the US Federal Reserve’s interest rate decision later this month. Last month, the US central bank raised rates by 25 basis points, bringing the target range to 3.75–4.00 percent, the first hike in three years.
Economists are divided over whether the Fed will raise rates again or hold them steady. According to CME FedWatch, which tracks the likelihood of monetary policy decisions, there is a 52.9 percent chance that rates will remain in the 3.75–4.00 percent range, while a 47.1 percent chance of a quarter of a percentage point hike that would bring them to 4.00–4.25 percent.
The inflation data puts pressure on Republicans before the midterm elections on November 3. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll showed that about 78 percent of Americans blamed US President Donald Trump’s policies for price increases.
US markets trended downward following the inflation report. The Nasdaq fell 0.8 percent and the S&P 500 dropped 0.6 percent, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was roughly flat in midday trading.
articles.summary:
United States consumer prices rose to 3.7 percent in September, driven largely by surging petrol costs and increasing pressure on the Federal Reserve regarding future interest rate hikes.

### Key Points
- Annual inflation accelerated to 3.7 percent in September, up from 3.4 percent in August, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
- Petrol prices surged 9.1 percent monthly and 34.2 percent annually, accounting for over half of the total Consumer Price Index increase.
- Shelter costs rose 0.4 percent, while computer software and accessory prices jumped 28 percent due to heavy investment in AI infrastructure.
- The Federal Reserve faces a split decision on interest rates, with a 47.1 percent market probability of a quarter-point hike later this month.
- US stock markets reacted negatively to the report, with the Nasdaq falling 0.8 percent and the S&P 500 dropping 0.6 percent.

### Why it Matters
This inflation data complicates the economic landscape ahead of the midterm elections and forces the Federal Reserve to weigh cooling price growth against potential market instability. Persistent energy and technology costs suggest that inflationary pressures remain broad, influencing both consumer sentiment and upcoming monetary policy decisions.

articles.title: Cisco Warns of Active Attacks Exploiting New Critical Secure Email Gateway Vulnerability
articles.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
articles.content:
Attackers are exploiting a critical flaw in Cisco Secure Email Gateway that lets a sender with no login write files to the appliance's operating system, Cisco said in an advisory on Wednesday.
The attacker sends an email with a crafted attachment through the gateway and, if it succeeds, could then run commands as root. The appliance filters an organization's email for spam, malware, and other threats, and only a gateway with the File Reputation service enabled and a Content Scanner Tools package older than version 25.3.0.5525 is vulnerable.
The fix has been shipping since September 14 in AsyncOS 15.5.5-014 and 16.5.0-780, the builds Cisco listed as fixed in a hardening release that day, which the company now says covered this flaw. It also arrives as a Content Scanner Tools update, version 25.3.0.5525 or later, which installs without a software upgrade or a restart.
Cisco found the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-76519 (CVSS score: 9.8), in its own internal security scanning and became aware of the attacks in October. The advisory does not say how many devices were attacked, who is behind the attacks, or whether the attackers obtained root on any of them.
Cisco has contacted customers of its managed Secure Email Cloud service whose devices showed "indicators of possible compromise" and says it is engaged in remediation and recovery. Administrators of those managed gateways may not have the command-line access needed to run the compromise check below, and Cisco has already deployed the fixed scanner there, so they need no action to get the fix.
Who Is Exposed
Both conditions must hold. The File Reputation service, part of the Advanced Malware Protection (AMP) feature that handles attachments, must be enabled and assigned to a mail policy, and the Content Scanner Tools version must be earlier than 25.3.0.5525.
Physical and virtual gateways on vulnerable AsyncOS releases are affected. Secure Email and Web Manager and Secure Web Appliance are not.
To check the first condition, open Mail Policies > Incoming Mail Policies > Advanced Malware Protection, or the same path under Outgoing Mail Policies, choose a mail policy, and look at the Enable File Reputation box. To check the second, run contentscannerstatus at the CLI, which shows the version and when it was last updated.
How to Fix It
The quickest route is the scanner update. Gateways with automatic Content Scanner Tools updates turned on need no action once the update has applied, so confirm with contentscannerstatus that the version is 25.3.0.5525 or later rather than assuming it arrived.
Where automatic updates are off, run contentscannerupdate at the CLI, or turn them on under Security Services > Service Updates.
The full AsyncOS fix is in these first fixed releases:
- 15.5: 15.5.5-014
- 16.0: no fixed build. Migrate to a fixed release.
- 16.5: 16.5.0-780
- Content Scanner Tools (all licensed and supported AsyncOS releases): 25.3.0.5525 or later
Cisco recommends that any gateway earlier than 16.5 move to 16.5.0-780. A 16.0 gateway on 16.0.4-302, the build that fixed September's SQL injection flaw, is not fixed for this one, and the advisory does not list which releases count as licensed and supported for the scanner update. For a 16.0 gateway that stays on 16.0, the scanner version shown by contentscannerstatus is the only confirmation the advisory offers.
There is no workaround. For a virtual appliance that shows signs of compromise, Cisco's guidance is a rebuild with new credentials, and it warns that upgrading a compromised instance destroys the forensic data and logs.
How to Check for Compromise
Cisco's check for attempted exploitation is one command on the appliance: grep "System Security" system_logs. It returns one of three messages:
- System Security: Suspected compromise indicator was found. Contact TAC for further recommendations. Compromise detected. Follow the recovery steps below.
- System Security: Security scan did not complete. Contact TAC for further recommendations. Contact Cisco's Technical Assistance Center (TAC).
- System Security: No compromise indicator was found. No compromise detected by this check. Upgrade if the device is on an affected release.
Run it on every member of a cluster. A clean result is not proof: an attacker with root could remove or hide evidence, so also check firewall and network logs outside the device for unexpected uploads to external IP addresses or downloads from malicious ones. The advisory does not say what the scan looks for.
If a Device Is Compromised
For a physical appliance, Cisco asks customers to contact TAC and to enable remote access so its engineers can investigate. For a virtual appliance, its steps are:
- Preserve forensic data first. Upgrading a compromised instance destroys its logs and evidence.
- Deploy a new virtual machine on a fixed release.
- Rebuild the configuration without importing any previous configuration file.
- Renew the credentials and cryptographic material on the appliance, then keep monitoring for unusual behavior.
Cluster members authenticate to each other with SSH key pairs. A compromised member's private keys could give the attacker a way into the others, so Cisco recommends restoring every member of a cluster that contains at least one compromised appliance. Secure Email Cloud customers it has contacted are asked to renew credentials and cryptographic material where possible.
The September Release
This is the second Secure Email Gateway flaw Cisco has confirmed under attack in a month. On September 14 it disclosed CVE-2026-76461, a SQL injection flaw in the gateway's email parsing that could let an unauthenticated sender run commands as root through a crafted email.
That flaw affects every configuration and was added to CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day. The two flaws sit in different parts of the software and have different log checks, and Cisco has not linked the attacks.
The same day, Cisco published a hardening release for the gateway and for Secure Email and Web Manager that grouped internally found bugs into five umbrella CVEs by weakness class: CVE-2026-76440, CVE-2026-76441, CVE-2026-20353, and CVE-2026-76443, each scored 9.8, and CVE-2026-76442 at 7.5. Each score is the highest among the bugs in that class, and the advisory carried the 15.5.5-014 and 16.5.0-780 builds.
Cisco updated that advisory on Wednesday, and it now says "Two of them are known to be actively exploited": the file-write flaw, which sits in the path traversal class, and the September SQL injection flaw, which sits in the improper neutralization class. It is not aware of attacks on the other bugs in the release.
Under a disclosure policy Cisco set out in June, bugs fixed in hardening releases share grouped CVEs, and a flaw gets its own CVE when, among other reasons, it is known to be exploited. The file-write flaw was fixed in September inside the path traversal group and received its own advisory on Wednesday.
It is also the third root-level flaw in these appliances that Cisco has confirmed exploited since December, when a China-linked group that Cisco Talos tracks as UAT-9686 used a zero-day in the spam quarantine feature, CVE-2025-20393, that Cisco patched in January.
articles.summary:
Cisco has issued an advisory regarding a critical vulnerability in its Secure Email Gateway that allows unauthenticated attackers to execute commands as root via malicious email attachments.

### Key Points
- The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-76519, carries a critical CVSS score of 9.8.
- Affected appliances must have the File Reputation service enabled and Content Scanner Tools version older than 25.3.0.5525.
- Administrators can remediate the flaw by updating to Content Scanner Tools version 25.3.0.5525 or installing AsyncOS releases 15.5.5-014 or 16.5.0-780.
- Cisco has confirmed active exploitation of the flaw and is currently assisting compromised customers with remediation and recovery efforts.
- Users can check for potential compromise by running the "grep 'System Security' system_logs" command via the appliance's command-line interface.

### Why it Matters
This flaw represents the third root-level vulnerability in Cisco Secure Email Gateways to be exploited in the wild since December, highlighting a persistent security risk for enterprise email infrastructure. Because successful exploitation grants attackers full control over the appliance, organizations must prioritize immediate patching to prevent unauthorized access and potential data breaches.

articles.title: Banks are now trying to offload the AI data center debt they just underwrote
articles.author: Janet Harrison
articles.content:
JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, SMBC and MUFG are quietly shopping pieces of the AI debt pile they helped build, a sign the lenders closest to the money have started hedging their own bet.
Six months ago, banks were racing each other to underwrite data center loans tied to Oracle, Meta and the rest of the AI buildout. Now some of the same banks are trying to get that debt off their books. JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, SMBC and MUFG have been exploring significant risk transfers, according to a report from the Financial Times. These are deals that let a bank keep a loan on paper while shifting its riskiest slice to outside investors. The banks are doing this because they are bumping up against internal limits on how much AI-linked exposure any one lender can hold.
One case shows how stuck this has gotten. A group of banks including JPMorgan and MUFG has spent more than six months trying to distribute $38 billion in construction debt tied to a Texas and Wisconsin data center project leased to Oracle, Bloomberg has reported. Some lenders are now willing to sell pieces of it to non-bank buyers at a discount, just to move it. Six months is a long time to sit on debt nobody underwrote to hold forever.
Matthew Moniot, co-head of credit risk sharing at Man Group, told the Financial Times the deal sizes involved are "out of scale to anything we've thought about, ever." That is not a hedge-fund manager talking down a trade he wants no part of. It is someone whose job is pricing exactly this kind of risk, saying the numbers no longer fit any model he has used before.
Oracle is the clearest tell. Its five-year credit default swaps, the cost of insuring against the company defaulting, climbed to around 151 basis points in early October, levels last seen in 2009, according to market data cited by Bloomberg. S&P had already cut Oracle's credit rating to BBB-, a single notch above junk, back in July. The company is reportedly targeting more than $40 billion in additional debt and equity this fiscal year. That is on top of the $18 billion in bonds it sold in a single day last September, and the money is needed to keep funding its Texas, Wisconsin and New Mexico sites.
Oracle sued Wisconsin's Public Service Commission over a rule that could force it to post more than $7 billion in collateral for its Port Washington data center campus. The fight helped push S&P to cut Oracle's credit rating to BBB-, one notch above junk, as the company's AI spending outpaces its cash flow. - Oracle Wisconsin data center collateral dispute - utilities regulator $7 billion lawsuit
Demand for that paper has thinned out, too. Bonds from Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle now trade at a premium to similarly rated non-AI corporate debt. Order books for their offerings have shrunk from roughly five times the amount on sale back in February to under two times by July, Bloomberg has reported. That is the difference between a bond that sells itself and one a bank has to work to place.
None of this is happening in isolation. The 10-year Treasury yield hit 5.304% this month, its highest since 2002, after a $39 billion auction cleared at 5.30%, the highest auction yield since 2000. The Federal Reserve's own September meeting minutes named AI-related corporate borrowing as a contributor to that move. Capital Economics argues the bigger driver is plain old inflation and government deficits, not tech company bond sales. Whoever is right about the cause, the effect is the same for anyone trying to finance a data center right now: the risk-free rate they are borrowing against just got a lot more expensive.
Frankly, the mechanics here matter more than the headline number. Banks do not sell down debt they are confident in. They sell down debt when they are worried about concentration, which is exactly what "approaching internal limits" means in plain English: too much of this bank's balance sheet is now one bet on one sector holding up. Spreading $120 billion of AI infrastructure spending across special purpose vehicles was supposed to make that risk easier to swallow. That is the structure Oracle, Meta, xAI and CoreWeave have all used to keep debt off their own balance sheets. Instead the risk is turning up at the banks that financed the SPVs in the first place.
The investors who still want in have gotten pickier about where. Capital is rotating toward data centers leased to investment-grade hyperscalers like Microsoft and Google, and away from weaker credits, Bloomberg has reported. That is exactly why CoreWeave-leased paper prices at 7.00% to 9.875%, against the 5.70% to 7.875% that hyperscaler-leased bonds command, per bond market data compiled by CCIR. A smaller, less capitalized AI infrastructure company trying to raise debt next quarter is now competing for the same nervous pool of lenders as Oracle. Except without Oracle's balance sheet or its existing customer base to point to.
That's the part of this story that does not show up in a single day's stock move. The AI boom still runs on the assumption that credit stays open indefinitely at reasonable terms. Six months of a bank struggling to sell $38 billion in loans is the clearest evidence yet that assumption is being tested in real time, not in some theoretical downturn still years away.

Major banks including JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley are offloading AI-related data center debt as they reach internal exposure limits and face cooling investor demand for tech infrastructure loans.

### Key Points
- JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, SMBC, and MUFG are seeking risk transfers to move AI-linked debt off their balance sheets.
- Banks have struggled for six months to distribute $38 billion in construction debt tied to Oracle data centers in Texas and Wisconsin.
- Oracle’s credit rating was downgraded to BBB- by S&P, sitting just one notch above junk status due to high AI spending.
- Demand for AI-related corporate bonds has weakened, with order books shrinking significantly since February.
- Yields for bonds leased to smaller firms like CoreWeave are trading at a premium compared to those leased to major hyperscalers.

### Why it Matters
The difficulty banks face in offloading these loans suggests that the massive capital requirements for AI infrastructure are beginning to strain traditional lending capacity. If credit markets continue to tighten, smaller AI firms may struggle to secure the funding necessary to sustain their rapid growth and capital-intensive operations.

articles.title: U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering
articles.author: BrianKrebs
articles.content:
The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.
On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.
As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.
The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.
“Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”
In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.
TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted new “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.
Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s sanctions against the platform were ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.
“A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”
As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said.
Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.
Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.
Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent company Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara.
That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara.
articles.summary:
The United Kingdom has imposed economic sanctions on the cryptocurrency platform Cryptomus for facilitating illicit financial activities and helping the Russian government circumvent international economic restrictions.

### Key Points
- The U.K. sanctions freeze all Cryptomus assets held in British banks and prohibit domestic companies from conducting business with the platform.
- Additional virtual payment services targeted by the U.K. include VexPay, TokenSpot, and Tsunami Payments.
- Cryptomus, previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox, rebranded as Heleket following a CAD $176 million fine from Canadian regulators for money laundering.
- Blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs reported that Cryptomus processed over $7 billion in transactions since 2022, including funds linked to human trafficking and terrorism.
- Investigations revealed the platform utilized a network of fake regulatory bodies and shell companies to operate under the guise of legitimate financial services.

### Why it Matters
These sanctions represent a significant escalation in the effort to dismantle the infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy by targeting the specific payment processors used for illicit transactions. By moving beyond unenforceable monetary fines to direct operational bans, the U.K. is setting a new precedent for how Five Eyes nations can collectively disrupt global cybercrime networks.

Former FTX Europe chief targets U.S. tokenized stock trading with new SEC exemption
Nasdaq-listed Perpetuals.com is the second company to pursue a U.S. tokenized stock marketplace under the SEC's new framework, following a joint venture between OKX and NYSE parent ICE.
- Nasdaq-listed Perpetuals.com plans to offer tokenized U.S. stocks under the SEC's new innovation exemption, following an earlier proposal from an OKX–ICE joint venture.
- CEO Patrick Gruhn co-founded Digital Assets AG, which developed stock-linked tokens for crypto exchanges including Binance and FTX before being acquired by FTX Group.

A Nasdaq-listed fintech company led by a former FTX Europe executive is planning to bring tokenized U.S. stocks trading onto blockchain rails under the Securities and Exchange Commission's (SEC) new regulatory framework.
Perpetuals.com (PDC), headed by CEO Patrick Gruhn, filed a notice on Wednesday that it plans to operate a tokenized securities venue under the SEC's five-year "innovation exemption," which allows certain marketplaces to trade U.S. stocks on public blockchains without registering as traditional securities exchanges.
The move makes Perpetuals.com the second company to pursue a marketplace under the exemption, following OKXICE, a joint venture between crypto exchange OKX and New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) parent Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), which last week filed plans for round-the-clock trading of more than 60 tokenized U.S. stocks.
The exemption, introduced in September, allows certain marketplaces to trade U.S. stocks on public blockchains without registering as traditional securities exchanges. It requires tokens to carry the same shareholder rights as ordinary shares, including dividends and voting rights, while giving companies 30 days to object to having their shares traded on a tokenized securities venue.
A return to tokenized stocks
The move marks a return to tokenized equities for Gruhn and his team, who helped develop some of the earliest stock-linked tokens offered by crypto exchanges including Binance and FTX in 2021.
Gruhn co-founded Digital Assets AG, a Swiss-based tokenization company that worked with German investment firm CM-Equity to bring digital tokens linked to stocks such as Tesla and Coinbase to crypto traders. Digital Assets AG was later acquired by FTX Group, becoming part of FTX Europe, which Gruhn led before the crypto exchange group's collapse in November 2022.
Those early products differed from the securities envisioned under the SEC's new framework. While they offered price exposure to underlying shares, Binance's stock tokens did not provide voting rights. Binance discontinued the offering in July 2021 amid regulatory scrutiny, including concerns raised by German regulator BaFin over the lack of a published securities prospectus.
"The Perpetuals team has long been trailblazers in tokenization, and this expansion into the U.S. allows us to further utilize our platform and deep expertise," Gruhn said in a statement.
The company already provides trading technology for Perpetual Markets MTF, a Cyprus-based marketplace licensed under Europe's MiFID II framework that also received authorization under the EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation in August.
The firm reported $65.2 million in total assets at the end of April, while posting a $17.6 million net loss during its fiscal year.
It also announced an agreement with Datavault AI earlier this year to support trading infrastructure for planned tokenized commodity offerings involving copper, gold and other physical assets, with more than $300 million in targeted issuance.
How the new trading venue would work
According to the public notice shared with CoinDesk, Perpetuals' U.S. marketplace will be operated by Kephas Corporation, a Delaware-based subsidiary. Trading would take place through permissioned automated market maker (AMM) liquidity pools, initially on Kronos X Public, an Ethereum-compatible layer-2 blockchain developed by the company.
AMMs use smart contracts and liquidity pools to facilitate trades between buyers and sellers instead of traditional exchange order books. Each pool would pair a tokenized U.S. stock with a digital asset, initially expected to be a form of USDC , allowing eligible investors to trade shares against the Circle-issued U.S. dollar-pegged stablecoin.
Perpetuals has not set a firm launch date yet. Trading could begin in mid-November at the earliest following the required 30-day period after the public notice, a company spokesperson told CoinDesk, depending on the completion of market-data and compliance arrangements, smart-contract security reviews and other preparations.
The company also plans to publish updated disclosures, including live smart-contract addresses, before trading begins, the spokesperson added.

articles.title: More Nothing smart glasses rumors suggest we might see two variations
articles.author: nickodiaz@sbcglobal.net (Nickolas Diaz) , Nickolas Diaz
articles.content:
What you need to know
- Rumors on social media claim Nothing is working on two smart glasses variations: one with a camera and one without.
- The "audio-equipped" version will reportedly let users place/receive calls and feature transition lenses.
- The camera version would offer similar capabilities to the audio-only one; however, it may feature translation capabilities, ChatGPT, and more.
- Earlier rumors this year suggested Nothing's CEO Carl Pei moved the company down this route with a potential release in 2027.
Nothing has made Android phones, headphones, and earbuds. However, recent rumors claim the company wants to branch out into smart glasses.
Rumors got underway on Bluesky by tipster Roland Quandt, who claims Nothing is working on a pair of smart glasses (via GSMArena). The tipster suggests the brand could launch two variations of its smart glasses: one with a camera and one without. Regarding the "audio-equipped" glasses, rumors purport Nothing's take could feature "auto-tinting photochromic lenses."
Otherwise known as "transition lenses," Nothing's smart glasses could darken (like sunglasses) when outside before clearing once you're inside. Quandt adds that these glasses would closely integrate with your phone's AI assistant and let users place/receive calls.
The alternative is the alleged camera-equipped version. Rumors on Bluesky state this pair would also provide translation capabilities and ChatGPT. There's little else about these alleged Nothing-branded smart glasses, so take these rumors with a grain of salt.
Nothing Glasses 1 (remember that?)
This would be the second time we've heard rumors about Nothing smart glasses (or a Nothing Glasses 1, as we've joked before). Earlier this year, a report claimed that Nothing CEO Carl Pei began making moves within the company to bolster the development of AI smart glasses. It was alleged that these lenses would feature a camera, speaker, and microphone.
Compared to what we've seen on Bluesky, some of these aspects could be separated. That report suggested that these smart glasses wouldn't be able to "handle everything" on their own. They would lean/rely heavily on your phone. For example, it was speculated that the glasses would rely on your phone for "the cloud to handle AI processing." It's unclear if things have changed, but Nothing might reveal these glasses in 2027.
It'll be interesting to see how Nothing handles a camera on smart glasses. We've seen the major backlash Meta has received. Cameras on smart glasses raise serious privacy concerns for many people. No one wants to be recorded constantly without their consent.

I'm really interested in what Nothing smart glasses would look like. I like the design its given its phones. It's different, and might seem like an acquired taste to some. I wonder if Nothing would go the transparent route, or would it try and match whatever design its next phones are going with? A unified direction could work out nicely for a brand that's already turning heads with its aesthetic.
